title: Selling Ourselves: A Critical Analysis of POPIA in the Age of Synthetic Data Markets
affiliations: University of Pretoria

detail.title: Selling Ourselves: A Critical Analysis of POPIA in the Age of Synthetic Data Markets
detail.abstract: The global synthetic data market is projected to exceed USD 2 billion annually, and South African citizens' personal information is increasingly among its raw materials. This article argues that the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA) contains a structural loophole in its de-identification and anonymisation framework that synthetic data commerce systematically exploits. By tracing the journey of personal data from lawful collection through synthesis to commercial resale, the article demonstrates that POPIA's all-or-nothing exclusion of de-identified information from regulatory protection fails to account for the re-identification risks inherent in synthetic datasets. A threshold question-whether data synthesis constitutes 'de-identification' within POPIA's section 1 definition at all-is examined and answered in the negative: synthesis generates new data rather than deleting identifying information from existing records, yet the current framework lacks the conceptual vocabulary to capture this distinction. Drawing on empirical research demonstrating the vulnerability of synthetic data to reconstruction attacks, comparative analysis of the GDPR and EU AI Act, and the constitutional right to privacy under section 14 of the Constitution, the article contends that POPIA's current framework is constitutionally inadequate and cannot be saved by the section 36 limitations clause. South Africa's multilingual data landscape-characterised by codeswitching, dialectal variation, and small-population language groups-renders this vulnerability especially acute. The article concludes with six reform proposals directed at closing the loophole, including the adoption of a functional anonymisation test and the extension of further processing limitations to derived datasets.

title: How Digital Technologies Reshape the Diffusion of Hydrogen Refueling Infrastructure: A Dual-Layer Evolutionary Game Perspective
affiliations: Beijing Normal University, Beijing Normal University and Peking University

detail.title: How Digital Technologies Reshape the Diffusion of Hydrogen Refueling Infrastructure: A Dual-Layer Evolutionary Game Perspective
detail.abstract: The widespread deployment of hydrogen refueling stations (HRS) is critical for a viable hydrogen economy. However, existing literature largely overlooks the co-evolutionary dynamics between firms and consumers amid digital transformation. This study proposes a novel framework—integrating evolutionary game theory with a dual-layer heterogeneous complex network—to model the asymmetric adaptation shaping HRS diffusion. We incorporate digital penetration by evaluating its impact on transparency, platform incentives, costs, and the social propagation of green preferences. Our results reveal that digitalization accelerates initial HRS diffusion by optimizing information flow and reducing uncertainty. While platform incentives stimulate enterprise construction, they exhibit diminishing marginal returns as network externalities saturate. Notably, the coupled firm-consumer system displays strong path dependence: despite early acceleration, enterprise participation converges to a partial equilibrium of roughly 50%, highlighting structural constraints against full-scale deployment. By embedding digital enablement into cross-layer evolutionary dynamics, this study advances socio-technical diffusion theory and offers actionable policy insights for synchronized digital-physical infrastructure planning.

title: Same Model, Different Politics? How Language Shapes AI Ideology
affiliations: Universidad Torcuato Di Tella - School of Business,  and

detail.title: Same Model, Different Politics? How Language Shapes AI Ideology
detail.abstract: Recent work measures ideological positioning and drift in large language models (LLMs), but typically assumes that those measurements are invariant to the language of evaluation. This paper tests that assumption using the full Political Compass questionnaire in English and Spanish across three generations of OpenAI models, together with a benchmark comparison against recent Qwen and Mistral releases. Using matched item-level responses, we estimate within-model Spanish-English displacement and assess how language choice affects cross-model ideological comparisons. We find that measured ideological coordinates remain in the same broad region of the ideological space across languages, but are not language-invariant. Spanish-English shifts differ in sign and magnitude across models and axes, and in several cases amount to a substantial share of the inter-model dispersion typically interpreted as ideological drift in English-only audits. We interpret these results as evidence that ideological evaluation in multilingual LLMs is not language-invariant, and that measured ideological placement depends on the language of elicitation. The main implication is methodological: ideological drift should not be treated as a language-invariant property of a model, but as a measured outcome conditional on language choice and instrument design. Multilingual audits should therefore report language-specific placements and within-model cross-language displacement rather than extrapolating from English-only measurements.

title:
The Token Governance Trap 
A Constraint-Based Diagnostic Architecture for Organizational Readiness and Value Attribution Under Goodhart's Law

detail.title:
The Token Governance Trap 
A Constraint-Based Diagnostic Architecture for Organizational Readiness and Value Attribution Under Goodhart's Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Kwarsick Consulting LLC and the creator of THE WHEEL Framework and WHEEL OS, which are discussed in this paper. No external party influenced the analysis, conclusions, or model specification. The paper is an independent conceptual and diagnostic architecture paper. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could have inappropriately influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this paper. The manuscript is a conceptual architecture and diagnostic-specification paper. It does not report research involving patients, human subjects, private organizational data, or identifiable participant data. The 100-scenario examination discussed in the paper uses constructed conceptual scenarios and does not constitute human-subject research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author through Kwarsick Consulting LLC.

detail.abstract:
Token consumption is becoming one of the primary instruments through which organizations attempt to monitor, budget, and govern enterprise AI adoption. Quota systems, billing dashboards, per-employee thresholds, usage targets, and agent-level consumption controls promise visibility into AI economics. Yet visibility is not governance. When token consumption becomes the managed target, organizations risk converting a useful cost signal into a distorted proxy for AI value.

This paper names that distortion the Token Governance Trap. Grounded in Goodhart’s Law and the organizational-readiness logic of THE WHEEL Framework, the paper argues that token governance fails when organizations treat consumption data as evidence of adoption quality without first diagnosing whether humans can distinguish purposeful from performative use, connect consumption to outcomes, authorize high-value exploration, and update governance from observed use patterns. The predictable result is not cost discipline. It is quota avoidance, compliance gaming, adoption chilling, and budget conflict between finance and technology leaders.

The paper develops three connected arguments. First, token governance is vulnerable to Goodhart distortion because token volume is easier to measure than AI-generated value. Second, the emerging economics of agentic AI intensify this vulnerability because autonomous and parallel agent architectures can increase token consumption by orders of magnitude while making human attribution harder. Third, token governance is therefore not only a financial-control problem. It is an organizational-readiness and human-governance-capacity problem expressed through financial metrics.

To address this gap, the paper proposes the Token Governance Readiness Model (TGRM), a candidate diagnostic architecture for evaluating whether token consumption is governable, attributable, and defensible before quota policies are imposed. The model defines Defensible Token Consumption as a function of Base Token Exposure, a WHEEL-derived Organizational Readiness Constraint, and Value Attribution Capacity. The model is not presented as a validated predictive instrument. It is a falsifiable structural proposal that specifies its assumptions, measurement requirements, validation path, and conditions for revision or rejection.

The paper further distinguishes the role of THE WHEEL and WHEEL OS. THE WHEEL provides the primary organizational-readiness diagnostic for human adoption behavior. WHEEL OS supplies the agentic-governance extension required when consumption decisions are generated by autonomous systems operating beyond direct human pacing. The practical implication is direct: organizations that impose token quotas before building readiness and attribution capacity may reduce visible consumption while destroying the exploratory, high-value use needed to justify AI investment.

A 100-scenario conceptual examination across Healthcare, Finance, Aerospace, Manufacturing, Government, and Tech sectors is reported as an internal coherence and face validity exercise. The examination produces sector-differentiated diagnostic patterns and shows that set-minimum reporting materially changes the interpretation of binding constraints. The examination does not constitute empirical validation; it specifies what empirical validation would require.

title: Signaling Product Authenticity with Inspection Services on the Second-hand E-commerce Platforms
affiliations: Tianjin University of Finance and Economics, Nankai University and Tianjin University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Signaling Product Authenticity with Inspection Services on the Second-hand E-commerce Platforms
detail.abstract: With the rise of transactions, asymmetric information about authenticity poses challenges for identifying and combating counterfeits. In response, platforms launch inspection services to provide endorsements for goods. However, their impact on platform profitability and seller pricing is still unclear. We investigate the decisions of heterogeneous sellers on whether to adopt inspection services and how to optimize profits and pricing between price and inspection signals. Using a signal game model, we confirm the conditional substitution and complementary relationship between two signals. Compared to price, the effectiveness of inspection services depends on the dynamic matching of inspection fees and counterfeit quality. We further found that there are potential loss traps for sellers using inspection services with the low inspection fee and inferior quality. One inference is that higher inspection fees can cause screening barriers, while lower inspection fees can easily lead to signal dilution. Finally, the paper emphasizes that competition in second-hand goods may reduce incentives for authentic sellers to adopt inspection services. The dual-signal mechanism and lower inspection fee will improve the welfare of all parties involved. This work supports sustainable development goals by promoting the efficiency of second-hand transactions and decision-making on price and service signaling mechanisms.​

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Coordination, Trust, and Cascading Failures

detail.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Coordination, Trust, and Cascading Failures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares the following: Rizwan Tanveer is employed as Principal Consultant at DTS Solution (Beyon Cyber), a cybersecurity consultancy operating in the Gulf Cooperation Council region. The frameworks and standards discussed in this paper, including the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, the OWASP AIVSS, the CSA MAESTRO framework, the Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit, and ISO/IEC 42001, are publicly available reference materials, and DTS Solution does not hold a financial interest in any specific framework or vendor referenced. This paper was prepared as part of the author's doctoral research at Walsh College and does not represent a commissioned consulting deliverable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval is not applicable. This paper is a narrative literature review based on publicly available primary sources. No human participants, patient data, or animal subjects were involved in the research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background. Agentic artificial intelligence systems, defined by their capacity to reason, plan, and act autonomously through external tools and environments, represent a categorical shift in the operational profile of deployed AI. Architectures grounded in reasoning-and-acting paradigms, plan-and-execute decompositions, and tool-augmented designs have moved from research prototypes into enterprise deployment within three years, yet the security, safety, and governance literature has not kept pace with the speed of operational adoption.

Purpose. This paper synthesises the contemporary literature on agentic AI architectures, autonomy taxonomies, emergent behaviours, memory and state management, and evaluation methodologies. It positions agentic AI as a distinct security and governance category requiring frameworks not satisfied by predictive AI controls, large language model controls, or traditional software assurance practices.

Approach. The paper adopts a narrative literature review methodology drawing on authoritative primary sources, including the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2025), the Cloud Security Alliance MAESTRO framework (2025), the DeepMind Levels of AGI autonomy taxonomy (Morris et al., 2024), foundational agent architecture research (Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), and the emerging agentic red-teaming and evaluation literature.

Findings. Three structural findings are advanced. First, agent architectures introduce attack surfaces (tool invocation, memory persistence, multi-step reasoning trajectories) that have no direct analogue in either traditional software or non-agentic AI systems. Second, autonomy is best treated as a continuum, operationalised through delegation boundaries, rather than as a binary property, with distinct security implications at each level. Third, evaluation methodologies designed for static models systematically underestimate risk in dynamic agentic systems, requiring red-teaming approaches that test for emergent behaviours, goal drift, and cascading failures across multi-step trajectories.

Implications. Practitioners deploying agentic AI require architecture-aware governance: tool-invocation controls, memory-hygiene practices, autonomy classification at the system-design stage, continuous behavioural monitoring, and red-teaming methodologies tailored to multi-step agent operations. The paper provides a structured reference for translating architectural choices into security and governance controls.

title: A Study on the Identification of Manipulative Design in Subscription and Payment Interfaces of Digital Consumer Platforms and Its Behavioral Effects
affiliations: NB Brother Corp, Vernon

detail.title: A Study on the Identification of Manipulative Design in Subscription and Payment Interfaces of Digital Consumer Platforms and Its Behavioral Effects
detail.abstract: Structural design considerations on subscription and checkout pages-like default options, delayed fee display, and winding upways-can affect how users make a decision and the cost of operation, without changing the contents of the transaction. This paper builds interface risk features based on 66, 261 interface samples of approximately 9, 300 applications in the Rico dataset, with 86, 021 Q&A pairs and 34, 812 interface screenshots of ScreenQA, which delivers interface risk features in the dimensions of button prominence ratio, fee notification hierarchy, path depth, and operation step size. Methodologically, we derive structural relationships using interface hierarchy parsing and graph structure modeling and integrate multimodal representation learning to determine the semantic locations of fees and subscriptions. In the experiments, samples were separated into a high-risk (top 18 percent) and a low-risk (bottom 22 percent) group according to the distribution of risk indexes and the outcomes were compared to the rule-based identification model and the traditional classification model. Findings indicated that the high-risk interface identification task had an AUC of 0.893 and an F1 score of 0.841 with the proposed model, which was an improvement of 8.37 and 10.52, respectively, over the rule-based methods;In terms of behavioral effects, the mean exit path length of high-risk interfaces was higher by 27.6% compared to the low-risk group, the cancellation success rate decreased by 14.8%, and the fee comprehension error rate rose by 9.21 percentage points, indicating that interface structure has a significant impact on consumers' autonomous decision-making.

title: A Study on Return Optimization in E-commerce for Complex Consumer Goods Driven by Installation Information Quality
affiliations: NB Brother Corp, Vernon

detail.title: A Study on Return Optimization in E-commerce for Complex Consumer Goods Driven by Installation Information Quality
detail.abstract: This study deals with the problem of non-quality returns in e-commerce for complex consumer products due to installation understanding bias, and proposes a return optimization approach based on the quality of installation information.Unlike the previous research, which focuses mainly on price, logistics, review sentiment, and customer attributes, this study introduces the quality of installation information into the return analysis framework. It systematically characterizes front-end cognitive factors-including step completeness, text image consistency, terminology clarity, visual guidance intensity, and adequacy of risk warnings-and, building upon return predictions, further identifies the net effect of optimizing installation information to differentiate between improved and genuine interventions.From a methodological point of view, the study uses BERT for semantic coding of post-purchase consultation texts, return cause descriptions and user feedback; uses XGBoost to construct a return risk forecasting model; explains key drivers in combination with SHAP; and uses Double Machine Learning to estimate the real effect of optimizing installation information on return rates.The experimental data set includes 14 months of business records, 52 product models, 6,480 product page interactions, 2,730 after-sales queries, 1,186 return records, and 920 installation instruction versions. Even after adjusting for product price, model complexity, and customer purchasing experience, the optimization of installation information still resulted in a consistent 11.6% decrease in return, a 33.4 per cent reduction in post-purchase enquiries, and a 22.1 per cent increase in customer satisfaction with the usability of products. This study offers an interpretable and quantitative analysis framework to reduce the non-quality of returns and to increase the transparency of product information.

title: Resolving the Interoperability Deadlock: Deterministic Shared-State Coordination in Australian e-conveyancing
affiliations: and Victoria University

detail.title: Resolving the Interoperability Deadlock: Deterministic Shared-State Coordination in Australian e-conveyancing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information. Formal human research ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

detail.abstract:
Interoperability within Australian e-conveyancing has traditionally been approached as a system integration problem centred on API connectivity and bilateral data exchange between independently operated Electronic Lodgement Network Operators (ELNOs). However, such approaches do not intrinsically guarantee deterministic agreement, atomic settlement, or consistent legally governed transaction state across independent institutional participants. The suspension of the national Direct Connect interoperability initiative highlighted the structural limitations of reconciliation-based coordination in high-value settlement environments requiring synchronised legal and financial state transition.

This paper reframes interoperability as a deterministic coordination problem rather than solely a communication or integration challenge. It proposes the Shared-State Coordination Mesh, a governance-aware distributed coordination architecture in which transaction validity is established through coordinated pre-commit validation of shared transaction state. The proposed model combines canonical transaction representation, composite Delivery-versus-Payment (DvP) coordination, Hybrid Notary Cluster validation, Conditional Finality, and deterministic reconciliation within a unified coordination framework.

The architecture embeds institutional authority directly within settlement coordination processes through role-constrained validation involving State Land Registries, financial institutions, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), ARNECC, and prudential oversight functions.

A prototype implementation developed using the R3 Corda permissioned distributed ledger platform was evaluated using a scenario-based Design Science Research methodology. The evaluation examined atomic settlement enforcement, state uniqueness preservation, delegated validation behaviour, bounded coordination continuity under temporary authority unavailability, and deterministic rollback under authoritative rejection conditions. The results demonstrate that interoperability can be achieved through governance-aware shared-state coordination enforced prior to ledger commitment rather than through post-execution reconciliation between independently maintained systems of record.

The paper contributes to interoperability theory by demonstrating that high-value regulated settlement environments require architectures capable of enforcing agreement before state transition occurs. It further shows that interoperability in such environments cannot be reliably achieved through integration alone, but requires governance-aware coordination mechanisms capable of preventing independently governed participants from committing conflicting legal and financial states.

title: Seeing in the Dark: Towards A Broad Construction of the Access to Data Provisions of the DSA
affiliations: Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Paris (Sciences Po) - Sciences Po Law School - Ecole de Droit de Sciences Po and Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)

detail.title: Seeing in the Dark: Towards A Broad Construction of the Access to Data Provisions of the DSA
detail.abstract: The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the most ambitious effort taken by liberal democratic nations to regulate social media platforms. One of the main ways it does this is by establishing various transparency obligations applicable to all platforms and search engines, as well as a specific transparency and data-sharing regime for the largest platforms and search engines, defined by the number of users. Specifically, Article 40 of the DSA grants vetted researchers access to data “for the sole purpose of conducting research that contributes to the detection, identification and understanding of systemic risks in the Union.” This article argues that Article 40's requirement for the requested data to be “necessary and proportionate” to conduct a specific type of research may hinder effective research. Indeed, researchers have been denied broad access – or any access to data – on privacy or confidentiality grounds before (Bontcheva, 2024). Consequently, researchers have limited prior knowledge of social media impacts and thus may have limited knowledge about what data, exactly, they need. Drawing on cutting-edge social media research, we explain why vetted researchers may thus need broad access to social media data to meet the objectives of the DSA. More specifically, we argue that researchers need access to system-level data, meaning data that captures how an entire digital system or platform operates, not just the activity of individual users. Consequently, we propose an interpretation of the DSA's data request requirements that would enable researchers to study the online political landscape of EU member states effectively.

title: A-Index: Rethinking Scholarly Influence When Your Audience is an Algorithm
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Boston - College of Management

detail.title: A-Index: Rethinking Scholarly Influence When Your Audience is an Algorithm
detail.abstract: An increasing number of people encounter academic ideas not through direct engagement with primary literature, but through AI-generated syntheses that selectively retrieve, interpret, and present research on their behalf. In this context, a scholar's influence is no longer determined solely by how often peers cite their work in academic journals, but by whether their ideas are represented in the AI systems that now mediate knowledge at scale. The result is a new and largely unmeasured dimension of scholarly influence: AI-mediated influence, defined as the degree to which a researcher's work shapes what AI systems retrieve, synthesize, attribute, and communicate to the world. This paper proposes the A-Index (AI-mediated Influence Index) as a framework for understanding and measuring this new form of influence. This paper argues that understanding AI-mediated influence empowers researchers to disseminate their work more effectively, reach broader audiences, and ensure their contributions are accurately represented in the AI systems. The risk, however, lies in institutionalization: once adopted as an official evaluation criterion, any metric rewards those with resources to optimize and penalizes those without. The goal of this paper is not to create another metric for institutions to adopt, but to raise awareness of a transformation that is already underway.

title: An SLO-Driven Reliability Framework for Cloud-Native Data Platforms

detail.title: An SLO-Driven Reliability Framework for Cloud-Native Data Platforms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The research involved no human participants, no animal subjects, and no collection or processing of identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background. Cloud-native data platforms now sustain mission-critical analytical processing, event-driven workflows, and enterprise data services at scale. These systems operate under stringent performance and availability demands, where marginal degradations in latency, throughput, or freshness can cascade into significant business consequences and Service Level Agreement (SLA) breaches. Despite the widespread adoption of distributed architectures-microservices, container orchestration, and stream-processing frameworks-reliability practices for data platforms remain predominantly reactive, responding to failures through alerting and incident escalation rather than proactively governing system behaviour against predefined Service Level Objectives (SLOs). 
Objective. This paper proposes the SLO-Driven Reliability Framework (SDRF), a structured framework that aligns cloud-native data platform architecture, observability, and incident response with continuous SLO enforcement. The SDRF is offered as a design proposal intended to shift reliability engineering from a corrective posture to a preventive and adaptive one, enabling continuous alignment between system behaviour and agreed service commitments.
 Approach. The SDRF comprises three integrated components: (1) the Hierarchical SLO Definition Model (HSDM), which structures SLOs across business, platform, and indicator tiers and captures dependency propagation across pipeline components; (2) the Dynamic Observability Engine (DOE), which performs continuous, multi-signal telemetry collection and real-time error budget computation; and (3) the Adaptive Reliability Controller (ARC), which executes auditable remediation actions in response to SLO violations or projected threshold breaches. The paper presents the architectural rationale for each component, the data contracts that bind them, and a proposed evaluation methodology for empirical validation in subsequent work. 
Contribution. The SDRF provides a principled, component-level reliability governance framework deployable across mainstream cloud-native data platform toolsets. By embedding SLO enforcement into the structural architecture of the platform rather than retrofitting it through monitoring configurations, the framework offers site reliability engineers (SREs), data platform engineers, and cloud architects an actionable design pattern for moving beyond reactive incident management toward continuous, measurable reliability assurance. Empirical validation of the framework is identified as the principal direction for future work.

title: Save Money, Build Talent, and Defend Communities: A Whole-Of-State Cybersecurity Guidebook

detail.title: Save Money, Build Talent, and Defend Communities: A Whole-Of-State Cybersecurity Guidebook

declarations.funderStatement: The Public Interest Cybersecurity Program at the Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC) is generously supported by Craig Newmark Philanthropies and Okta for Good, whose championing of cybersecurity for organizations big and small enables the pursuit of research projects like this one.

detail.abstract:
As part of a growing “whole-of-state” cybersecurity strategy, many states are piloting cyber defense programs that rely on local talent to provide hands-on assistance to fill critical gaps in the cyber defenses of communities. These programs lean on civilian participation to help bolster defenses, often by upskilling students and deploying local skilled volunteers to save money, develop the local cybersecurity workforce, and build resilience. However, these programs cannot succeed in a vacuum; they need financial and administrative support from state leaders.

In this guidebook, the UC Berkeley Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC) Public Interest Cybersecurity Program highlights a collection of community cyber defense programs: cybersecurity clinics, regional security operation centers (RSOCs), and state cyber corps. The guidebook then outlines the return on investment of these programs. 

Key insights from this guidebook explore how community cyber defense programs:


Addressing the operational realities of these programs, the guidebook explores shared aspects of successful programs, as well as common hurdles and examples of how to overcome them. Zooming out, the guidebook then highlights how these programs can work together to create a cohesive and resilient state cyber ecosystem. Through case studies centered on initiatives in Texas, Wisconsin, and New Jersey, the paper shows how a network of programs collaborating and sharing intelligence can be a force multiplier for a state’s investment in local cyber defense. 

This guidebook provides a path forward for state legislators, chief information security officers (CISOs), chief information officers (CIOs), and governors to double down on their whole-of-state cybersecurity strategy by investing in and connecting their local cyber defense programs.

title: The Pro-Worker AI Benchmark: Measuring Whether Large Language Models Augment or Replace Human Intelligence

detail.title: The Pro-Worker AI Benchmark: Measuring Whether Large Language Models Augment or Replace Human Intelligence
detail.abstract: Large Language Models are now embedded in professional workflows, raising a measurement gap: do these systems augment human cognition or substitute for it? This paper introduces the Pro-Worker AI Benchmark (PWB), translating the human-AI complementarity literature into eleven measurable dimensions of pro-worker behavior. The benchmark spans 320 evaluation instances across seven professional domains: 200 single-turn behavioral probes, 16 multi-turn scenarios, and 40 adversarial stress tests. Seven open-weight LLMs from six families are evaluated with a three-judge panel and five runs per prompt. Baseline PWI sits between 25.4 and 39.2, indicating largely substitutional default behavior. A proworker system prompt raises PWI to 56.9-82.3 (∆ = +24.6 to +46.2, Cohen's d = 0.59-1.30), with the effect persisting at multi-turn (d = 1.61) and adversarial (d = 1.41) layers (p < 10-37). While durable improvements belong at the model layer, deployment-layer steering offers a practical short-term path. The near-term lever for pro-worker outcomes lies with the practitioners and organizations configuring the alignment surface. All prompts, rubrics, scoring code, and per-run results are released.

title: Deep learning-based reconstruction of plasmonic scattering spectra from sparse spectral measurements
affiliations: University Mohammed First, University Mohammed First, University Mohammed First and University Mohammed First

detail.title: Deep learning-based reconstruction of plasmonic scattering spectra from sparse spectral measurements
detail.abstract: Reconstructing scattering spectra from limited spectral measurements is a recurring need for plasmonic nanostructures, both in numerical workflows where full-wave simulations are computationally expensive and in experimental settings where broadband scans can be slow, bandwidth-limited, or sparsely sampled. We address this problem with a supervised deep learning framework targeted at gold nanoridge dimer-on-mirror structures. Two complementary masking schemes are studied: a contiguous spectral window, which forces the model to extrapolate beyond the observed region, and a random sparse mask, which reduces the task to interpolation between scattered observations. Three architectures with different inductive biases are compared on a dataset of 1307 COMSOL-simulated scattering spectra: a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) with dilated kernels, and a one-dimensional U-Net, a U-shaped encoder–decoder network with skip connections. We find that no architecture is universally optimal. Under contiguous masking, the MLP outperforms both convolutional models, with R2 ≈ 0.98 from only one third of the spectral range, because its dense connectivity provides a global receptive field suited to long-range extrapolation. Under random sparse masking, all three architectures reach R2 ≥ 0.989, but the CNN matches the larger U-Net while using roughly five times fewer parameters. A bandwidth ablation in the contiguous case shows that one third of the spectral range is sufficient for high-fidelity reconstruction, with diminishing returns beyond about 40% visibility, and a visibility ablation in the random case shows that 25–30% of the spectral points is sufficient for reliable reconstruction. The architecture-task coupling identified here gives a concrete design rule for sparse spectral acquisition and neural post-processing pipelines in nanophotonics.

title: Anticompetitive Entry with Multimarket Contact
affiliations: American University and American University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Anticompetitive Entry with Multimarket Contact
detail.abstract: We build a model where a firm’s entry into one market creates multimarket contact (MMC) with the incumbent firm, since they both compete in a second market as well. We show that entry can facilitate tacit collusion across markets, raising prices in the second market without reducing them in the market that was entered. This contrasts with the usual policy presumption that entry is pro-competitive but is consistent with empirical evidence showing anti-competitive impacts of MMC. Antitrust regulators may therefore wish to include changes in multimarket contact among the criteria used to evaluate market entry.

title: Subsidizing Inequality Government Subsidies and Rising CEO-Employee Pay Disparities
affiliations: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) (Formerly University of Texas-Pan American), Marquette University - Department of Finance and Ball State University - Miller College of Business

detail.title: Subsidizing Inequality Government Subsidies and Rising CEO-Employee Pay Disparities
detail.abstract: Do government subsidies benefit workers, or do they primarily enrich corporate executives? This paper investigates the effects of government subsidies on the CEO–employee pay gap using US data from 2000 to 2021. We apply regression analysis, difference-in-differences, nearest neighbor matching, and instrumental variable technique to assess how subsidies influence the CEO–employee pay disparity. We demonstrate a positive and persistent relationship between subsidy receipt and the CEO–employee pay gap. Furthermore, we show that this effect is stronger in firms with weak corporate governance and among large subsidy recipients. Our findings highlight how government intervention can exacerbate agency problems, offering new insights into executive behavior and the unintended consequences of public subsidies.

title: Workplace Responses to Perpetration of Family and Domestic Violence: A Global Scoping Review
affiliations: Curtin University, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, affiliation not provided to SSRN and The University of Western Australia

detail.title: Workplace Responses to Perpetration of Family and Domestic Violence: A Global Scoping Review
detail.abstract: Introduction: Family and domestic violence (FDV), including intimate partner violence, affects workplace safety through spillover impacts on workers, organisations, and occupational health systems. To date, workplace responses to the problem of FDV have largely focused on supporting victim-survivors, with little scholarly insight into how employers respond to workers who perpetrate FDV. Method: A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which examined existing evidence from workplace policies, practices, and organisational mechanisms addressing FDV perpetration by workers. Peer-reviewed studies and high-quality grey literature on workplace responses to perpetration of FDV were systematically searched across multiple databases and online sources and 19 documents on workplace responses to FDV perpetration were analysed. Results: Findings from the scoping review reveal four dominant insights across the literature: 1. Perpetration of FDV is a major workplace problem, yet responses are under-researched; 2. Workplaces employ wide-ranging and varied responses, from zero tolerance dismissal of perpetrators to responsibility avoidance; 3. Responses lack a solid evidence-base and regulatory frameworks to address the problem remain weak; 4. Practical strategies are provided to better manage risk, strengthen safety, and reduce violence. Conclusions: Our findings underscore the need for clearer organisational guidance, evidence-based strategies, and robust regulatory frameworks to strengthen workplace responses to FDV perpetration and improve occupational safety outcomes. Practical applications: Effective workplace responses to perpetration of FDV should consider work design factors, referral pathways and confidentiality protections which are guided by graduated accountability models and regulatory frameworks.

title: Manipulation or Market Stress? On-Chain Evidence from Nine Asia-Pacific Cryptocurrency Shocks
affiliations: Hitit University

detail.title: Manipulation or Market Stress? On-Chain Evidence from Nine Asia-Pacific Cryptocurrency Shocks
detail.abstract: We examine whether Asia-Pacific cryptocurrency misconduct and enforcement events impair Bitcoin price discovery and whether on-chain transaction anomalies can distinguish manipulation-driven disruptions from market stress reactions. Using raw transaction data from the XBlock-BTC dataset and the AWS Public Bitcoin Dataset, we construct an On-chain Anomaly Score (OAS) derived from Isolation Forest applied to four block-level features — transaction density, fee rate anomaly, large-value transfer intensity, and input-output asymmetry — across ten major Asia-Pacific events spanning 2011 to 2022. We link OAS to a Price Discovery Efficiency (PDE) index constructed from return autocorrelation and variance ratio metrics. Panel OLS results reveal a period-trend effect in which later events occur in a more mature market, confounding pooled identification of event-driven PDE impairment. Mann-Whitney tests provide partial support for pre-event anomaly elevation: three events — the Bithumb Hack (2017), OKEx Freeze (2020), and China Mining Ban (2021) — exhibit statistically significant pre-event OAS elevation (p < 0.01), consistent with informed on-chain repositioning ahead of public disclosure. Difference-in-differences and interaction regressions find directionally consistent but statistically insignificant differential effects of enforcement versus misconduct events, constrained by the small enforcement subsample. Robustness checks confirm stability across alternative window specifications and PDE components. The findings suggest that unsupervised on-chain anomaly detection carries forensic value as an early warning indicator for financial intelligence units operating in Asia-Pacific jurisdictions without requiring labeled transaction data or off-chain surveillance infrastructure.

title: How does Local Government Financing Vehicles Shareholding Affect the Maturity Mismatch of Corporate Investment and Financing?
affiliations: Ningbo University and University of Nottingham, Ningbo - University of Nottingham Ningbo China

detail.title: How does Local Government Financing Vehicles Shareholding Affect the Maturity Mismatch of Corporate Investment and Financing?

keywords: Maturity Mismatch of Corporate Investment and Financing Activities

detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of systemic financial risk prevention and the pursuit of a virtuous cycle in the real economy, whether Local Government Financing Vehicles (LGFVs) shareholding alleviates maturity mismatch of corporate investment and financing activities is a question of critical importance, not only for the development of individual firms but also for high-quality macroeconomic growth. Using a sample of A-share listed firms in China’s Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges from 2009 to 2021, this paper theoretically analyzes and empirically tests the impact of LGFVs shareholding on corporate maturity mismatch. The empirical results indicate that LGFVs shareholding can significantly alleviate corporate maturity mismatch and the finding is still robust across a series of empirical checks. Mechanism analyses show that LGFVs shareholding improves firms’ long-term financing capacity through a resource-provision channel and restrains overinvestment through a governance optimization channel, thereby collectively mitigating corporate maturity mismatch. Further analysis indicates that the mitigating effect of LGFVs shareholding is more pronounced in firms with concentrated LGFVs shareholding, firms controlled by non-state-owned capital and firms under higher economic policy uncertainty. Our findings provide valuable theoretical insights for policy design aimed at optimizing corporate financial behavior and curbing corporate financial risks.

title: Enrollment Management under Deep Uncertainty: An Entropy-Driven Bayesian Decision Architecture for UK Higher Education
affiliations: University of Bedfordshire

detail.title: Enrollment Management under Deep Uncertainty: An Entropy-Driven Bayesian Decision Architecture for UK Higher Education
detail.abstract: UK universities face compounded enrollment uncertainty from demographic plateau, volatile international postgraduate taught demand, and a frozen domestic fee cap, while capital commitments and programme restructuring are largely irreversible within a planning horizon. We introduce an entropy-driven Bayesian Decision Theory (BDT) architecture, formalised as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), for annual enrollment-driven financial management in Research Intensive higher education institutions (HEIs). The architecture uses the Shannon entropy of the posterior demand-regime belief as an automatic caution regulator: under high regime uncertainty the system hedges toward prior expectations and favours reversible strategic postures; as Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) evidence accumulates and entropy collapses, it progressively commits to the posterior-optimal strategy. A satisficing gate imposes a hard viability constraint that prevents catastrophic over-commitment when Low-regime probability is elevated, and an option-value mechanism penalises irreversible decisions before regime identity has been established. Empirical calibration uses HESA student and finance data from four Russell Group universities (Warwick, Exeter, Leeds, Bristol) over 2014/15--2024/25. Monte Carlo simulation ($n = 500$) shows that the architecture achieves risk-adjusted Pareto dominance over five comparators: statistically equivalent expected reward to the best comparator strategy (mean 349.2 vs.\ 360.7, $p = 0.986$) with 0.9 percentage points lower distress probability---approximately 4--5 fewer financial-crisis paths per 500 simulations. Entropy collapse following Bayesian belief updating alone explains 17--30\,\% of the reward premium over non-belief strategies. The architecture produces zero distress across all five initial belief scenarios tested, including a pessimistic 50\,\% prior on the Low regime. The calibration pipeline uses only HESA and Office for National Statistics (ONS) open data and is designed for annual redeployment.

title: DaPV: Domain-Adaptive Pointwise Vortex-Induced Vibration Detection
affiliations: University of Seoul and University of Seoul

detail.title: DaPV: Domain-Adaptive Pointwise Vortex-Induced Vibration Detection
detail.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) of long-span bridges is usually monitored using 10-min statistical features and empirical thresholds, which limits temporal resolution and can delay the detection of emerging or weak events. Recent deep-learning approaches have shown that pointwise sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models can identify VIV at the sampling rate of acceleration measurements, but they typically require labeled data for each bridge and often fail when transferred to structures with different dynamic properties. In practice, only a few bridges experience clear VIV events during the monitoring period, while many others provide only non-VIV data and exhibit noticeable cross-bridge domain shift due to differences in natural frequencies. This study proposes DaPV (Domain-adaptive Pointwise VIV detection network), an attention-based LSTM seq2seq model that adapts a pointwise VIV detector from a VIV-experienced source bridge to one or multiple target bridges that provide only non-VIV segments. DaPV employs a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss computed on LSTM features to align the non-VIV feature distributions between source and target-domains, while the classifier is supervised solely by pointwise labels from the source bridge. The domain gap is quantified by the difference in first-mode natural frequencies, and controlled target-domains with prescribed frequency shifts are synthesized by resampling real monitoring data to emulate various cross-bridge scenarios. Three experimental settings are considered: single-target adaptation under a large modal-frequency gap, simultaneous adaptation to multiple targets using an averaged MMD strategy, and extrapolation to an unseen target beyond the trained frequency range. The results show that DaPV restores pointwise VIV detection performance in cases where a conventional attention-LSTM fails, stabilizes learning across multiple targets, and retains useful performance for unseen domains, demonstrating the potential of domain-adaptive pointwise VIV monitoring for long-span bridges.

title: Neutralising the curse of dimensionality: a neural transport-preconditioned MCMC framework for Bayesian structural identification
affiliations: Wuhan University of Technology and City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: Neutralising the curse of dimensionality: a neural transport-preconditioned MCMC framework for Bayesian structural identification
detail.abstract: Bayesian model updating offers a principled framework for calibrating structural models from measurement data, yet the underlying Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler becomes prohibitive as the parameter dimension grows and the posterior departs from a Gaussian shape. Multilevel kernel-density (KDE) proposals — standard in recent structural identification studies — succumb to the curse of dimensionality beyond roughly eight uncertain parameters. We introduce NeuTra-MCMC, a parallel MCMC framework that uses a normalising flow as a coordinate transport rather than a proposal density: posterior samples are obtained by random-walk Metropolis in a near-isotropic latent space, with exactness preserved through a single Jacobian determinant. A warmup-then-NeuTra schedule resolves the cold-start training problem, two-group cross-fitting preserves invariance under parallelisation, and an optional multi-proposal mechanism boosts acceptance. We prove detailed balance, ergodicity, and flow-reuse validity. On three D=10 analytical targets the method cuts posterior-mean error 84× on heteroscedastic geometries; on Lam et al.'s (2019) 19-storey sailboat-shaped building it recovers published modal MPVs within 9% per parameter and, at D=12, attains 2.8× lower mean error than multilevel KDE while retaining ~23.4% acceptance. The crossover dimension D ≈ 8 marks the practical decision boundary between KDE and NeuTra preconditioning.

title: UMSA-CSNet: A Deep Unfolding Network for Multi-Channel Compressive Sensing of Structural Vibration Signals
affiliations: Tongji University, Tongji University, Tongji University and Tongji University

detail.title: UMSA-CSNet: A Deep Unfolding Network for Multi-Channel Compressive Sensing of Structural Vibration Signals
detail.abstract: Multi-channel high-frequency vibration data in structural health monitoring (SHM) impose substantial demands on data storage and real-time transmission. Compressive sensing (CS) provides an effective means to alleviate this burden; however, conventional iterative reconstruction algorithms are often computationally expensive, while purely data-driven deep learning models typically lack explicit optimization structures and interpretability. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Unfolding-based Multi-channel Spectral Attention Compressive Sensing Network (UMSA-CSNet), an ISTA-inspired deep unfolding network for the compressed reconstruction of multi-channel structural vibration signals. By transforming the complex Fourier spectrum into a real-valued concatenated representation, the proposed framework enables measurement-consistency updates and collaborative prior learning to be performed within a unified and interpretable unfolding space. Specifically, a cross-sensor spectral prior module is embedded into each unfolding stage to exploit spectral sparsity and cross-sensor dependencies, where self-attention mechanisms and learnable soft-thresholding are jointly introduced to enhance joint reconstruction capability. The proposed method is validated on a numerical 3-DOF system, the Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) three-story frame benchmark, and field-measured data from a commercial wind turbine tower. Experimental results show that UMSA-CSNet consistently outperforms FISTA and MT-BCS in terms of reconstruction quality, dominant spectral preservation, preservation of inter-sensor correlation structures, and reconstruction efficiency. The proposed method provides an effective framework for low-rate acquisition and high-fidelity reconstruction of multi-channel vibration responses in SHM.

title: An integrated analysis of metal pollution in sandy beaches: Sediment quality, bioavalability and biological stress assessment. Case study: Taltal, Chile
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidad de Antofagasta and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: An integrated analysis of metal pollution in sandy beaches: Sediment quality, bioavalability and biological stress assessment. Case study: Taltal, Chile
detail.abstract: A study was conducted to assess the environmental risk in two sandy beaches of the Atacama Desert, northern Chile: Atacama beach (25°23’S; 70°28’W) and Cifuncho beach (25°39’S; 70°38’W). Multiple approaches were applied, including environmental indices, sequential BCR extraction, laboratory bioassays, and molecular analysis using Argopecten purpuratus as a bioindicator of toxicity. Heavy metal analysis in supratidal and subtidal sediments showed that Atacama presented concentrations ranging from 800 to 1,093 mg kg⁻¹ for Pb and from 1,212 to 1,977 mg kg⁻¹ for Cu. In contrast, Cifuncho exhibited significantly lower concentrations, ranging from 15.7 to 42.5 mg kg⁻¹ for Pb and from 88.8 to 94.5 mg kg⁻¹ for Cu. Environmental indices indicated a high degree of contamination and a high probability of toxicological effects at Atacama. BCR analysis reported bioavailable fractions between 26 and 35% for Cu and 9–15% for Pb, suggesting a greater probability of Cu transfer to biota. These results were consistent with laboratory bioassays, where scallops exposed to Atacama sediments reached 100% mortality within 96 h, together with higher Cu concentrations in tissues (70 mg kg⁻¹) and increased GST gene expression compared with other treatments. Overall, these findings indicate that pollution levels at Atacama beach are extremely high, mainly due to historical mining activities at the site, exceeding even other contaminated areas in the Antofagasta Region and posing adverse effects and toxicity risks to benthic biota.

title: DWCFL-DP: Dynamic Weighting and Closed-Form Aggregation in Federated Learning with Differential Privacy
affiliations: Hunan University of Technology and Business, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Hunan University of Technology and Business, Hunan University of Technology and Business, Hunan University of Technology and Business and Hunan University of Technology and Business

detail.title: DWCFL-DP: Dynamic Weighting and Closed-Form Aggregation in Federated Learning with Differential Privacy
detail.abstract: Federated learning protects data privacy by exchanging model parameters rather than raw data, but scalability and data heterogeneity introduce heavy communication over-head, slow convergence, and overfitting. We propose DWCFL-DP, a Dynamic Weighting and Closed-Form Aggregation framework with diﬀerential privacy that uses weight-shrinking aggregation and a closed-form training paradigm to improve stability and generalization on heterogeneous, large-scale Non-IID clients. DWCFL-DP reduces reliance on manual hyperparameter tuning by leveraging a closed-form aggregation paradigm and supports single-cycle local training via analytic aggregation rules, reducing communication and simplifying deployment. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under various Non-IID configurations demonstrate that DWCFL-DP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, convergence stability, robustness to malicious or corrupted clients, and communication efficiency. In particular, the proposed method achieves up to 10% improvement in global accuracy, reduces training time per round by approximately 69.82 seconds, and lowers total communication volume by over 45% compared with standard FedAvg. These results confirm that DWCFL-DP provides an eﬀective and scalable solution for privacy-preserving federated learning in heterogeneous and large-scale environments.

title: Social Ties and Bank Deposit Flows
affiliations: University of Alabama - Culverhouse College of Commerce & Business Administration and

detail.title: Social Ties and Bank Deposit Flows
detail.abstract: We investigate whether uninsured deposit flows are less sensitive to the performance of banks from regions to which their depositor-base regions have stronger social ties. Using a novel measure of Bank Social Proximity based on Facebook social network data, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in social proximity reduces deposit flow-performance sensitivity by approximately 50%, with the effect concentrated among poorly performing banks and significantly stronger when common factors drive bank performance. The effect weakens when strong political or religious ties already exist. Moreover, banks with greater social proximity experienced smaller stock price declines and less severe deposit outflows during the March 2023 banking stress. Overall, our findings highlight the role of social proximity in financial stability.

detail.title: Population-Level Biological Protection against Severe COVID-19 in West Africa: Findings from a 20,748-Participant Multi-Country Phased Seroepidemiology Study

detail.abstract:
Background: Africa seemed to have had low SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 morbidity and mortality. While several studies reported high SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity among healthy Africans, others hypothesized that this could have resulted from pre-existing cross-reactive antibodies.  Our study tracks trends in seropositivity across three West African countries during the Delta and Omicron pandemic waves using a validated test kit with 98.9% predictive accuracy, 97% sensitivity, and 99% specificity.

Methods: Cross-sectional studies were conducted across three West African countries (Burkina Faso, Ghana, and Nigeria) with study sites conveniently selected in each country. Using the validated immunoassay kits, with already published validation procedures, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies were detected in peripheral blood during the ‘Delta’ and ‘Omicron’ waves. Participants' demographic and clinical data were obtained using a semi-structured questionnaire, and the primary outcome was the proportion of each population with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.

Findings: Across the 3 countries, 20,748 participants were recruited, and the results showed SARS-CoV-2 IgG seropositivity ranging between 24.1% to 77.0%, which increased during the Omicron wave. All sites showed low self-reported vaccination rates, delinking seropositivity and vaccination. While there was a significant positive association between seropositivity and age across all sites, the association with other demographic factors was country-dependent, and most participants expressed positive opinions of vaccination.

Interpretation: This is one of the largest population-based SARS-CoV-2 seroepidemiology studies in Africa, confirming widespread mild SARS-CoV-2 infection in West Africa. This confirms a marked disconnect between high population exposure and low reported clinical burden, underscoring the need for strengthened community surveillance.

title: Beyond Screening: Evaluating the Clinical Transferability of AI Models to Complex Diagnostic Mammography
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Emory University, Emory University, Emory University, Emory University, Emory University, Emory University, Victoria University of Wellington, National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore (NUS) - Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, Emory University and Emory University - School of Medicine

detail.title: Beyond Screening: Evaluating the Clinical Transferability of AI Models to Complex Diagnostic Mammography

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Emory University (IRB0010801). The requirement for informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the analysis involving de-identified data. Reporting follows the STARD 2015 guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was, in part, funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Agreement No. 1OT2OD032581.

detail.abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence systems for mammography have demonstrated strong performance in screening populations, achieving diagnostic accuracy comparable to expert radiologists. However, their reliability in diagnostic mammography, which involves higher prevalence, non-standard protocols, and anatomically complex cases, has not been systematically evaluated.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study evaluating AI transferability from screening to diagnostic mammography at a single academic institution. We analysed 244,385 screening and 82,643 diagnostic examinations acquired between 2013 and 2020. Three AI architectures were compared: a vision-language foundation model (Mammo-CLIP), a standard convolutional neural network, and a medical foundation model (MedImageInsight). Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and specificity at a fixed sensitivity threshold of 68·1%.

Findings: All three models achieved comparable screening performance (AUC 0·78-0·81). When applied to standard diagnostic views, Mammo-CLIP and EfficientNet showed statistically significant AUC reductions (ΔAUC −0·09, p<0·001 and ΔAUC −0·08, p=0·011), whereas MedImageInsight maintained screening-level discrimination (ΔAUC 0·00, p=0·92). In patients with breast implants, specificity dropped by 21-51 percentage points and AUC fell to 0·69-0·76. MedImageInsight achieved the highest performance on spot compression views (AUC 0·84). Lesion localisation was poor across all cohorts (mean intersection over union 0·136). Performance was consistent across racial and ethnic subgroups.

Interpretation: AI systems validated on screening mammography cannot be safely deployed to diagnostic populations without targeted adaptation. The performance degradation in patients with breast implants, affecting approximately 10% of adult women, represents an important safety gap. Foundation models offer improved robustness for diverse imaging protocols compared with standard CNNs, but poor localisation accuracy raises concerns about clinical interpretability. Clinical implementations should incorporate explicit patient selection criteria and context-specific probability thresholds.

title: Latent Distress States, Financing Frictions, and Capital Structure Dynamics
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Latent Distress States, Financing Frictions, and Capital Structure Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether heterogeneity in capital structure adjustment reflects firms operating under different latent distress states. We distinguish between economic distress, which captures persistent deterioration in operating fundamentals and debt capacity, and financial distress, which captures liquidity shortages, refinancing pressure, and constrained access to external finance. We also identify mixed distress, where both mechanisms interact. Using a partial observability bivariate probit model, we estimate firm-year probabilities of latent distress states for U.S. publicly traded nonfinancial firms from 1993 to 2021 and incorporate these probabilities into dynamic leverage models. The results show that distress states have distinct implications for target leverage and speed of adjustment. Economic distress is associated with lower target leverage and faster deleveraging, particularly among highly levered firms, consistent with a structural reduction in sustainable debt capacity. Financial distress is associated with slower adjustment and persistent high leverage, suggesting that refinancing frictions restrict balance-sheet rebalancing. Mixed distress produces the strongest state dependence, consistent with a high-leverage trap in which operating weakness and financing frictions reinforce each other. External validation, panel VAR evidence, and indirect-cost tests indicate that the estimated states capture economically meaningful forms of corporate fragility. The findings imply that conventional leverage models may obscure important state dependence by pooling firms facing different sources of distress.

title: Central Clearing and the Transmission of Intermediary Capital Shocks in CDS Markets
affiliations: Swansea University, Swansea University and Swansea University

detail.title: Central Clearing and the Transmission of Intermediary Capital Shocks in CDS Markets
detail.abstract: This study examines how the transition to central clearing reshapes the transmission of intermediary capital shocks to the Credit Default Swap (CDS) term structure. Using latent level, slope, and curvature factors extracted via a dynamic Nelson–Siegel framework and applied to a dataset of single-name CDS contracts derived on 149 European and U.S. reference entities over the period 2008–2012, we find that central clearing significantly moderates the sensitivity of CDS spread components to dealer capital constraints. Specifically, the sensitivity of the level factor increases, while clearing anchors the term-structure slope, thereby mitigating the risk of curve inversion during periods of intermediary distress. At the same time, curvature sensitivity intensifies, concentrating shock transmission at intermediate maturities, with amplification especially pronounced for European reference entities. These results demonstrate that central clearing fundamentally alters the maturity dimension of credit risk pricing.

title: Entropy-Guided Resampling for Learning-Dynamics Improvementin Imbalanced Image Classification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Entropy-Guided Resampling for Learning-Dynamics Improvementin Imbalanced Image Classification
detail.abstract: Class imbalance remains a major challenge in image classification, particularly when minority classes contain visually ambiguous or fine-grained samples. Although transfer learning often provides strong baseline performance, it does not necessarily ensure a balanced learning trajectory across classes. This study proposes an entropy-guided resampling strategy that combines class rebalancing with uncertainty-based sample prioritization. Instead of duplicating minority-class samples uniformly, the proposed method preserves the original training samples and uses predictive entropy to select the additional duplicated samples required to balance each class. The method is evaluated across multiple image classification datasets by comparing baseline training, standard max resampling, and entropy-guided max resampling. The analysis emphasizes learning dynamics through AULC-F1, defined as the mean validation macro-F1 across validation checkpoints, together with best validation macro-F1 and balanced accuracy. Mean normalized entropy is also examined as a dataset-level descriptor of baseline predictive uncertainty. The results show that entropy-guided resampling improves AULC-F1 relative to the baseline across all evaluated datasets. Relative to standard resampling, the effect is dataset-dependent: clear gains are observed in UNODC and PathMNIST, marginal gains in HAM10000 and BloodMNIST, and no advantage in Zenodo and Wood. These findings indicate that entropy guidance is most useful when uncertainty-based sample prioritization contributes information beyond class-frequency correction alone. Mean normalized entropy helps characterize the uncertainty landscape, but it is not sufficient by itself to predict improvement, since gains also depend on within-class entropy heterogeneity, optimization behavior, and the informativeness of high-entropy samples. Overall, entropy-guided resampling offers a simple and practical mechanism for incorporating predictive uncertainty into imbalance-aware training, while its benefits should be interpreted as conditional rather than universal.

title: DeMamba: Deformable Convolution Meets Mamba for Local–Global Semantic Reasoning in Agricultural Segmentation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: DeMamba: Deformable Convolution Meets Mamba for Local–Global Semantic Reasoning in Agricultural Segmentation
detail.abstract: Agricultural scene understanding through semantic segmentation plays a crucial role in modern agricultural intelligence, supporting phenological analysis, yield estimation, disease assessment, and efficient crop management. However, agricultural environments present unique challenges, including foreground–background ambiguity, occlusions, phenological variation, and large intra-class scale variation. Recent advances in semantic segmentation, including CNNs, transformers, and Mamba-based architectures, have achieved significant progress; however, each paradigm still exhibits inherent limitations in balancing fine-grained local detail and global context reasoning. In this work, we propose DeMamba (Deformable convolution meets Mamba), a novel architecture that integrates deformable convolution-based local feature modeling with efficient Mamba-based global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Global Semantic State Validation (GSSV) module to enhance long-range dependencies and an Adaptive Local–Global Fusion (ALGF) gated mechanism to effectively combine local and global representations. Furthermore, a two-stage training strategy with gate supervision and structure-aware stage loss is employed to improve segmentation consistency. Extensive experiments on a challenging UAV-based rice panicle dataset show that DeMamba consistently outperforms existing SOTA methods across multiple metrics (including +1.00% IoU, +2.13% Acc) and panicle sizes ranging from +5.04% (tiny) to +3.36% (large) IoU. Additionally, consistent gains on other agricultural tasks datasets, namely NLB (disease) and WGISD (fruit) further validate the generalization capability and robustness of the proposed approach. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Mainstreaming Climate Action in Kenya's Coffee and Tea Value Chains: Climate Policy Integration and Green Trade under AfCFTA

detail.title: Mainstreaming Climate Action in Kenya's Coffee and Tea Value Chains: Climate Policy Integration and Green Trade under AfCFTA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Interest to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: No funding provided

detail.abstract: Kenya's coffee and tea sectors are central to rural livelihoods and export earnings but are increasingly exposed to climate variability and long-term climatic shifts. Despite growing policy attention, limited empirical work has examined how climate action is operationalised within export-oriented agricultural value chains and its implications for development outcomes. This study applies a qualitative policy analysis and secondary data synthesis to examine the mainstreaming of climate action in Kenya's coffee and tea sectors, drawing explicitly on the Green Supplement to Kenya's AfCFTA Implementation Strategy as a policy innovation case. The Supplement positions trade as a vehicle for climate resilience by integrating sustainable production, regulatory alignment, and green market access within continental trade frameworks. The analysis shows that climate risks-manifested through reduced yields, increased pest and disease incidence, and declining product quality-are already undermining sector performance and smallholder livelihoods. In response, the Green Supplement advances regenerative agriculture, sustainable consumption and production practices, and carbon sequestration through agroforestry as core adaptation and mitigation pathways. It further introduces a structured theory-of-change framework linking policy instruments, value chain interventions, and resilience outcomes. However, implementation gaps persist, particularly in financing, addressing non-tariff trade barriers, and ensuring equitable participation of women, who contribute up to 70% of labour yet remain structurally disadvantaged. By conceptualising climate action across absorptive, adaptive, and transformative capacities, this study demonstrates that integrating climate policy with trade frameworks can enhance resilience while strengthening competitiveness in sustainability-sensitive markets. The Kenyan case provides a scalable model for embedding climate resilience within trade-driven agricultural systems across Africa.

title: DamViT: A Multi-scale Vision Transformer for Damage Detection in Structural Health Analysis of Concrete Dams
affiliations: COMSATS University Islamabad, University of Oslo - Oslo University Hospital, Riphah International University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: DamViT: A Multi-scale Vision Transformer for Damage Detection in Structural Health Analysis of Concrete Dams
detail.abstract: Structural health analysis (SHA) of dams and water reservoirs is essential for ensuring their long-term safety, durability, and operational reliability. Conducting timely assessments, however, remains challenging due to practicing visual inspection methods are prone to persistent moisture, efflorescence, complex illumination conditions, and natural occlusions such as vegetation. These factors significantly reduce the robustness and consistency of automatic damage detection. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel multi-scale Dam Vision Transformer (DamViT) architecture specifically designed for robust and automated damage detection and segmentation. DamViT utilizes a dual-branch framework: a Coarse branch that efficiently identifies potential damage regions by capturing global context and a Fine-grained branch that performs high-precision segmentation and delineation of specific defects, namely cracks and spalling, by extracting localized, high-resolution features. To facilitate rigorous development and evaluation, we meticulously annotated and compiled a high-quality dataset comprising 5,000 high-resolution image patches (512 x 512 pixels) of dam surfaces. Thorough Experimentation on the test set demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed approach. For damage detection, DamViT achieves mAP of 0.92 for cracks and 0.95 for spalling, and for segmentation, it attains mAP scores of 0.72 and 0.80, respectively. These results outperform well-established approaches (e.g., U-Net, DeepLabV3+, DeepCrack, CrackFormer) and recent YOLO variants. The proposed DamViT advances the state-of-the-art in SHA by enabling timely and reliable damage detection for cost-effective long-term infrastructure maintenance.
