detail.abstract: Deeplearningmodelsinvisualtasksmayexploitunintendedcorrelationsindatasets rather than robust task-relevant cues, leading to performance degradation under out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Although shortcut learning has become an important issue in visual robustness research, existing approaches mainlydependontrained modelanalysisorverification ofpredefinedshortcut types, making them insufficient for identifying latent multi-dimensional shortcuts in new datasets before model training. To address this limitation, we propose a proactive multi-dimensional shortcut mining and verification framework that integrates shortcut discovery before model training, automatic dimension specific OOD sample construction and validation. For each dataset, the framework systematically mines shortcut risks across eight dimensions, including background, co-occurring objects, color, texture, pixel-level patterns, position, size, and angle. The mined shortcut cues are quantified by the Potential Bias Score (PBS), while model-level shortcut dependency is measured by the Shortcut Association Score (SAS) ongenerated OODsamples.SystematicexperimentsonWaterbirds,ColoredMNIST, Visual Genome, and a self-constructed compound-shortcut dataset demonstrate that the framework can identify dominant shortcut cues, reveal co-existing multi-dimensional shortcut structures, and distinguish dataset-level shortcut cues from model-level dependency. The results further provide practical guidance for dataset diagnosis, targeted data revision, and lightweight mitigation to improve OOD generalization.

title: Do Dedicated Freight Corridors Cause Economic Growth in India? A Difference-in-Differences Analysis

detail.title: Do Dedicated Freight Corridors Cause Economic Growth in India? A Difference-in-Differences Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare no financial interest or conflict of interest in this research work.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper is fully self-funded (all resources used are free of cost).

detail.abstract: We provide the first causal district-level evaluation of India's Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC), exploiting the staggered commissioning of 33 stretches across 49 districts between 2020 and 2026. Using monthly nighttime satellite luminosity for 568 Indian districts over 87 months, we find that DFC commissioning is associated with an average 4.5% reduction in local economic activity (β =-0.046, p = 0.004), driven by a short-run disruption effect that dissipates within six to twelve months. Heterogeneity analysis reveals the effect is entirely concentrated in Eastern DFC districts (β =-0.067, p = 0.006), while Western DFC districts show no significant response. This is a divergence attributable to the absence of complementary industrial infrastructure in the Gangetic Plain. Results are robust to Callaway-Sant'Anna correction, district-specific time trends, and placebo testing. Our findings suggest that freight rail infrastructure alone is insufficient to generate local economic spillovers in lagging regions without complementary investment in industrial capacity and last-mile connectivity.

title: The Ontological Boundary of Algorithmic Assessment: AI, Heidegger, and the Irreducibility of Identity in Executive Search

detail.title: The Ontological Boundary of Algorithmic Assessment: AI, Heidegger, and the Irreducibility of Identity in Executive Search

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author, Alessio Montaruli, is the Founder and Group CEO of KiTalent, an international executive search firm referenced throughout the paper as the applied context in which the philosophical argument becomes operational. KiTalent's published methodology, editorial work, and engagement models are cited as primary evidence for the practical implications of the argument. The author received no external funding for this research. The paper develops a philosophical position that is methodologically and commercially aligned with KiTalent's service model, and this alignment is disclosed throughout the paper itself.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper presents a philosophical and conceptual argument; it does not involve human or animal subjects, clinical data, or empirical research requiring ethics approval.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in recruitment and executive search to map markets, classify profiles, screen documents, organize signals, and accelerate data-intensive workflows. These uses are valuable. They increase visibility into candidate markets and can make the early phases of search more systematic. Yet the same representational power creates a category risk: organizations may begin to confuse candidate representation with candidate understanding. This paper develops a Heideggerian account of that boundary. Drawing on Heidegger's concepts of being-in-the-world, significance, care, publicness, idle talk, enframing, standing-reserve, and releasement, it argues that artificial intelligence operates most effectively on the level of already-public, already-formalized, and already-circulating intelligibility. It can map the visible field of talent, but it cannot perform the singularizing judgment required to assess identity-fit in a concrete executive mandate. The argument provides a philosophical grounding for the capability-identity distinction developed in KiTalent's research and methodology: soft skills belong to capability, while culture fit belongs to identity and must be read in relation to a specific organizational world. The paper also explains how this framework supports a set of KiTalent practices: AI can legitimately support talent mapping but should not replace consultant-led interviews; blind CVs are weak evidence in senior search; and Proof-First Search de-risks executive hiring by shifting proof from decontextualized representation to situated evidence.

title: Detecting Deposit Stress in Real Time: Rate Shock and Early Warning Model Performance
affiliations: University of North Florida

detail.title: Detecting Deposit Stress in Real Time: Rate Shock and Early Warning Model Performance
detail.abstract: This study asks whether supervisory CAMELS-based early warning systems can detect stress in real time when a new shock operates through unfamiliar mechanisms. We examine this question using the 2022-2025 rate shock as the empirical setting. Drawing on 1,001,495 bank-quarters of U.S. commercial bank data from 1992 to 2025, we compare three progressively richer specifications under a rolling expanding-window design across 13 out-of-sample quarters. Two modifications recover meaningful detection capacity: depositor composition augmentation dominates early in the episode before crisis observations accumulate, while regime conditioning gains advantage as coefficient shifts become identifiable. The depositor-composition model identifies 34 additional stressed institutions over the pooled benchmark, with hit rates reaching 55.9 percent against a 5.6 percent baseline. Overall, the results show that standard CAMELS architecture can be augmented to recover meaningful supervisory signals in real time, using data already available to supervisors.

title: Implementing UNSCR 2250 in West Africa: A Critical Policy Analysis of Liberia’s National Action Plan on Youth, Peace, and Security (2025–2030)

detail.title: Implementing UNSCR 2250 in West Africa: A Critical Policy Analysis of Liberia’s National Action Plan on Youth, Peace, and Security (2025–2030)
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the Liberia National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security (2025-2030) to evaluate its effectiveness in the localized implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution (UNSCR) 2250. Focus is placed on how the policy addresses the critical pillars of rehabilitation, mental health, and reintegration for young people in post-conflict Liberia. Adopting a qualitative policy analysis approach, the study evaluates the framework through the lenses of peacebuilding theory, youth participation theory, and policy implementation theory. The findings indicate that while the policy marks a significant stride in institutionalizing youth civic engagement, severe gaps remain regarding operational funding, concrete implementation coordination, and robust psychosocial support networks. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations to strengthen West African youth security policies, serving as a blueprint for implementing global mandates in fragile, post-conflict environments.

title: Multi-Objective Optimization of Double-H Finned Tube Heat Exchangers via CFD-DEM: Entropy Generation, Fouling, and Erosion Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU)

detail.title: Multi-Objective Optimization of Double-H Finned Tube Heat Exchangers via CFD-DEM: Entropy Generation, Fouling, and Erosion Analysis
detail.abstract: H-type finned tube heat exchangers are widely used in heat transfer process of dusty gas. Problems such as flow resistance, fouling and erosion are multiple constraints restricting the design of such heat exchangers. This study establishes a multi-objective optimization framework combining RSM, entropy weight method and NSGA-Ⅱ algorithm, and adopts the CFD-DEM coupled method to simulate a double H-type finned tube heat exchanger, aiming to balance its thermodynamic efficiency, erosion resistance and anti-deposition performance under gas-solid two-phase flow. Firstly, a quadratic polynomial response surface model was developed to quantitatively correlate five key parameters (tube spacing, fin width, fin fillet radius, gas velocity, particle diameter) with three critical performance indicators, namely total entropy generation (ΔSpro), erosion rate (verosion), and deposition rate (Rd). The effects of parameter coupling on entropy generation, fouling and erosion were analyzed in further detail, revealing clear trade-offs and synergistic effects between the parameters. The Pareto solution obtained via NSGA-II resulted in an optimized design that reduced total entropy generation from 0.005957 W/K to 0.005815 W/K, and the erosion rate from 45.28×10⁻¹² m/s to 37.76×10⁻¹² m/s, but the deposition rate increased from 13.14% to 15.05%. The comprehensive performance of the heat exchanger has been improved. This work provides an effective optimization method for the design of tube heat exchangers in gas-solid two-phase flow conditions.

title: Pre-feasibility Study on Business Opportunities for Women in a Changing Energy Value Chain in West Africa
affiliations: Maalexi Inc.

detail.title: Pre-feasibility Study on Business Opportunities for Women in a Changing Energy Value Chain in West Africa
detail.abstract:
This report culminates an effort to identify, evaluate, and evolve recommendations for improving women entrepreneurs across West Africa. It forms part of the ECREEE project — Pre-feasibility Study on Business Opportunities for Women in a Changing Energy Value Chain — funded by the NEPAD-IPPF, a multi-donor Special Fund hosted by the African Development Bank.

The project's mission is to ensure West Africa meets its goal of universal energy access for over 300 million people — by developing a gender-responsive regional energy market strategy that harnesses the entrepreneurial capacity of ECOWAS women to establish energy businesses and deploy energy technologies for the region's largely unserved population. It targets 16 women-led businesses across 4 ECOWAS countries, focusing on underfinanced SMEs, and is a direct product of the ECOWAS Policy for Gender Mainstreaming in Energy Access — targeting 25% women's participation in private sector energy by 2020 and 50% by 2030.

Challenges for women in West Africa span operational complexity, technological expertise, labour, and financial management — compounded by cultural pressures and limited technical know-how. Addressing these urgently is essential for women entrepreneurs to thrive in the evolving energy value chain.

Key Achievements

a) Created the first-ever formal database of women entrepreneurs in the energy value chain across West Africa's four largest economies.

b) Built a comprehensive understanding of women-led businesses across operational, commercial, technological, labour, legal, and financial dimensions.

c) Identified key challenges and developed tactical and strategic solutions to address them.

d) Collected primary field research data to support future women's entrepreneurship policy development.

e) Identified feasibility studies as replicable templates for regional expansion and diversification.

f) Equipped banks and funds with financial and operational profiles of women-led businesses to better design fit-for-purpose products.

g) Provided multilateral agencies and governments a framework for mainstreaming women in the fast-changing energy value chain.

h) Delivered actionable insights to women entrepreneurs on performance, improvements, and new growth opportunities.

i) United women entrepreneurs and ecosystem stakeholders to collaborate and collectively drive business growth.

title: Corporate Criminal Liability and Firm Value
affiliations: Northwestern University - Pritzker School of Law

detail.title: Corporate Criminal Liability and Firm Value

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming, Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization

detail.abstract: This paper explores the impact of corporate criminal law doctrine on firm value. I study stock market reactions to an Indian Supreme Court decision holding that a corporation’s mens rea (i.e., criminally culpable state of mind) is established when its controller has criminal intent. Companies controlled by individuals and families declined in value in response to this decision, likely because they had human controllers—dominant individuals or families—whose misconduct now left the firms vulnerable to prosecution. This value destruction is concentrated in business group companies, which are tightly controlled by founding families and whose reputation is linked to that of their controller. The effect is smaller for firms that have more foreign institutional ownership, and larger for consumer-facing firms. Firms with individual and family controllers relatively increased legal spending after the decision. Criminal liability’s effect on firm value is thus influenced by the identity of controllers, and institutional investors seem to be better ex-ante monitors of misconduct than consumers.

title: The perfect district heating modelling approach in energy system models: insights from an expert survey
affiliations: Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research ISI, , Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research ISI and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The perfect district heating modelling approach in energy system models: insights from an expert survey
detail.abstract: District heating (DH) networks based on renewable and excess heat sources are set to play a key role in the transition to a climate-neutral energy system. Model-based assessments analyse the role of DH in terms of demand, infrastructure, supply, costs, and the impact on the energy system. Various approaches are employed, ranging from simulation and optimisation of individual DH networks to large-scale energy system models (ESM) that consider multi-sector interdependencies, e.g. heat-electricity interactions via power-to-heat. While there are reviews of various aspects of ESM and of specific DH models, there is still a lack of insight into how DH is modelled in ESM that capture sector coupling across several regions, the EU or worldwide. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the modelling of DH in 13 large-scale, multi-sector ESM. The results demonstrate that some ESM model DH with a single grid per country, while others use several grids per model region. Additionally, the level of techno-economic detail varies: Some ESM cover over 16 DH generation technologies, others cover less than eight technologies. The DH demand is often given as an exogenous input parameter, whereas some ESM model it endogenously. While all models have distinct advantages, they also have shortcomings, indicating that there is room for improvement in modelling techniques to better capture the complexity of DH in large-scale, multi-sector ESM.

title: Technical Sustainability in Software Systems: An Empirically Grounded Research Agenda from the Brazilian Context
affiliations: State University of Maringá, State University of Maringá, affiliation not provided to SSRN, State University of Maringá, University of Castilla-La Mancha, State University of Maringá and State University of Maringá

detail.title: Technical Sustainability in Software Systems: An Empirically Grounded Research Agenda from the Brazilian Context
detail.abstract: Technical sustainability (TS) of Software Systems (SS) refers to the capacity of software systems to endure and evolve over time by preserving high internal quality. While it connects present-day decisions with long-term viability, little is known about how software practitioners understand and apply it within the Brazilian context. This study investigates perceptions, practices, and barriers associated with TS through a survey of 222 software practitioners, combining quantitative and qualitative analyses to derive a research agenda for advancing TS. The findings reveal high perceived importance and normative appreciation of the technical pillars of TS, but limited institutionalization and predominantly reactive adoption. Practices tied to short-term delivery cycles are prioritized, whereas activities essential for long-term evolutionary sustainment remain secondary and are frequently interrupted, even when recognized as important. This misalignment reflects sociotechnical tensions: TS requires continuity and incremental evolution, while organizations tend to operate under short cycles driven by immediate goals. Consequently, short-term prioritization emerges as a rational response to production constraints rather than negligence or lack of awareness. The main contribution of this study is a research agenda, grounded in practitioners' reported experiences, oriented toward understanding the organizational capabilities and governance mechanisms required to sustain TS over time. Although derived from the Brazilian context, this agenda addresses broader tensions that may also inform future research in other software development settings.​

title: Governance of Therapeutic Uncertainty Across Expedited Regulatory Systems: Comparative Lifecycle Governance Architectures, Institutional Legitimacy, and Reform Pathways in Contemporary Pharmaceutical Regulation

detail.title: Governance of Therapeutic Uncertainty Across Expedited Regulatory Systems: Comparative Lifecycle Governance Architectures, Institutional Legitimacy, and Reform Pathways in Contemporary Pharmaceutical Regulation

keywords: Global Lifecycle Governance Architecture Expedited approval

detail.abstract: Expedited regulatory pathways have transformed contemporary pharmaceutical governance by enabling earlier patient access to therapies addressing serious, rare, or life-threatening conditions. Although these mechanisms, including accelerated approval, conditional marketing authorization, adaptive licensing, reliance pathways, and real-world evidence integration, have expanded therapeutic access and innovation incentives, they have simultaneously intensified regulatory dependence on surrogate endpoints, incomplete clinical datasets, and evolving post-market evidentiary obligations. This review examines expedited approval systems through a comparative lifecycle governance framework, analysing how major regulatory authorities, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA), Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA), Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), operationalise therapeutic uncertainty across the medicine lifecycle. The manuscript argues that expedited pathways should not be understood solely as accelerated approval mechanisms, but rather as institutional governance architectures that redistribute evidentiary uncertainty from pre-market evaluation toward post-market oversight, enforcement, and lifecycle accountability. Through comparative analysis of conditional approvals, reliance systems, pharmacovigilance infrastructures, confirmatory trial enforcement, and regulatory modernisation initiatives, the review identifies substantial divergence in lifecycle governance capacity across jurisdictions. The paper further develops the concept of a Governance Failure Spectrum, illustrating how insufficient post-market oversight may progressively result in enforcement drift, institutional fragility, legitimacy erosion, and declining public trust. To address these challenges, the manuscript proposes a Global Lifecycle Governance Architecture (GLGA) integrating proportional oversight, evidentiary modernisation, reliance-sensitive governance, real-world evidence ecosystems, pharmacovigilance strengthening, artificial intelligence oversight, and international convergence strategies. The review additionally introduces an Expedited Regulatory Legitimacy Doctrine (ERLD), emphasising that the long-term legitimacy of expedited systems depends not on approval speed alone but on sustained lifecycle accountability, institutional transparency, adaptive evidence generation, and the preservation of public trust. By synthesizing regulatory science, governance theory, pharmacovigilance, artificial intelligence governance, and comparative institutional analysis, this manuscript reframes expedited approval systems as dynamic lifecycle governance ecosystems rather than isolated procedural acceleration tools. The proposed framework offers a governance-oriented foundation for future regulatory modernisation and international convergence in increasingly data-intensive and uncertainty-driven pharmaceutical environments.
