title: Calibrating the Visible: IFRS 18, IFRS 19, and the Governmentality of Disclosure Intensity

detail.title: Calibrating the Visible: IFRS 18, IFRS 19, and the Governmentality of Disclosure Intensity
detail.abstract: The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) issued IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements in April 2024 and IFRS 19 Subsidiaries without Public Accountability: Disclosures one month later, both effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Critical accounting research has established that accounting standards organize what is rendered visible in financial reporting, for whom, and in what form (Armstrong, 1994; Hopwood, 1987; Miller and O'Leary, 1987). Taking that insight as a starting point rather than restating it as a finding, this paper argues that the 2027 revision constitutes a theoretical development: a shift in the IASB's governmental rationality from universal disclosure to calibrated disclosure. The IASB's legitimacy as a transnational standard-setter has historically rested on the proposition that IFRS-compliant statements should be substantially equivalent across reporting entities (Botzem, 2012; Camfferman and Zeff, 2015; Richardson and Eberlein, 2011). IFRS 19 formally qualifies this proposition by introducing a graduated scale of disclosure intensity organized around entity-type classification. IFRS 18 specifies the upper bound of that scale, formalizing categories of operating performance and drawing management-defined performance measures into the perimeter of auditable disclosure. Through a Foucauldian discourse analysis of the IASB's official texts and effects analyses, this paper reads the two standards together as the joint institutionalization of a new governmental object: the calibrated architecture of disclosure intensity itself. This paper then traces the implications of this shift for the IASB's legitimacy claims and for the analytical vocabulary of critical accounting research.

title: Nexus Between Domestic Debt, Savings, and Economic Growth in Nigeria: A Conceptual and Theoretical Analysis
affiliations: and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Nexus Between Domestic Debt, Savings, and Economic Growth in Nigeria: A Conceptual and Theoretical Analysis

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and theoretical systematic literature review based entirely on secondary data and publicly available academic sources. No human participants, personal data, interviews, surveys, or experimental procedures were involved. Therefore, formal ethical approval was not required for this study.

detail.abstract: This study examines the nexus between domestic debt, savings, and economic growth in Nigeria using a conceptual and theoretical analytical approach. The study is motivated by persistent fiscal deficits, low domestic savings, and unstable growth performance in developing economies, particularly Nigeria. It adopts a systemic macro-financial perspective in which domestic debt, savings, and economic growth are treated as interdependent variables within a dynamic economic system. The study integrates Keynesian fiscal theory, neoclassical growth theory, endogenous growth theory, debt overhang theory, and financial intermediation theory to explain the interaction among the variables. It relies on established empirical and theoretical literature from indexed sources such as the World Bank, International Monetary Fund (IMF), and peer-reviewed journals. Findings from the literature show that domestic debt has a nonlinear effect on economic growth, while savings positively influence growth through capital accumulation and investment financing. However, excessive domestic debt may crowd out private investment and reduce savings mobilisation. The study concludes that the relationship among the variables is systemic, nonlinear, and feedback driven. The study recommends a balanced fiscal structure, improved savings mobilisation, and efficient financial intermediation to support sustainable economic growth in Nigeria.

title: Optimal Control of Battery–Supercapacitor Systems in EVs Using Real-Time GPS Data - A Hybrid Safe Reinforcement Learning Approach
affiliations: Seoul National University of Science and Technology, Seoul National University of Science and Technology and Seoul National University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Optimal Control of Battery–Supercapacitor Systems in EVs Using Real-Time GPS Data - A Hybrid Safe Reinforcement Learning Approach
detail.abstract: A hybrid energy storage system (HESS) that combines a lithium-ion battery (LiB) and a supercapacitor is increasingly regarded as a promising solution for electric vehicle (EV) power supply. In such systems, supercapacitors handle high-power demands, thereby reducing the power burden on the LiB and slowing its degradation. Despite this potential, prior studies on energy management systems (EMS) for HESS have not sufficiently addressed two critical issues. First, they remain limited to reactive control based on previous internal information, which constrains proactive control of the supercapacitor. Second, they do not adequately account for safety in the system dynamics with respect to battery temperature, current, state of charge (SoC) and supercapacitor SoC. To address these limitations, we propose a world models-based approach and a hybrid safe reinforcement learning (RL) framework. By leveraging real-time external information, such as GPS data, the proposed approach enables proactive control strategies within a world models framework. In addition, we propose a hybrid safe RL framework that integrates a safety filter with a Lagrangian method to derive an optimal policy under the efficiency-safety trade-off. Using real-world driving datasets, the proposed framework achieves a cost reduction of 6.68-20.00% compared with conventional RL and optimization baselines while guaranteeing safety.

title: Mandated Pay Transparency and Workforce Restructuring
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

detail.title: Mandated Pay Transparency and Workforce Restructuring

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This study is not involved in any personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations.
declarations.funderStatement: This study is not funded by other people or organizations.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether mandated pay ratio disclosure induces firms to restructure their workforce composition. Under the Dodd-Frank Act, U.S. publicly traded firms were required beginning in 2018 to disclose the ratio of CEO annual total compensation to the median employee's pay. Using a continuous difference-indifferences design that exploits cross-sectional variation in firms' initial disclosure pay ratios, I analyze online job posting data from Lightcast for a sample of publicly traded firms over 2013-2023. Firms with one standard deviation higher pay ratios post 7.8% less job ads after the disclosure. The reduction in job postings entails a substantial restructuring of hiring: They post significantly more job ads with wage disclosure and a work-from-home option, while reducing job ads for low-education and junior positions. These shifts in hiring composition are accompanied by a documented rise in median employee compensation and a decline in overall employment. The findings indicate that pay ratio disclosure induces firms to manage the reported figure through workforce composition rather than through genuine wage increases, paradoxically reducing job opportunities for the low-wage workers the mandate was designed to protect.

title: Heterogeneous Energy Storage-Supported Demand Response in Integrated Energy Systems: A Resilient Market-to-Delivery Framework under Compound Disturbances
affiliations: University of Canterbury, , Chitkara University, Khalifa University and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Heterogeneous Energy Storage-Supported Demand Response in Integrated Energy Systems: A Resilient Market-to-Delivery Framework under Compound Disturbances
detail.abstract: Heterogeneous energy storage systems are central to preserving flexibility delivery in cyber-physical integrated energy systems (IES) when market-cleared commitments must remain feasible under uncertainty, cyber disturbances, communication degradation, and real-time operational deviations. This paper proposes a resilience-oriented market-to-delivery framework for storage-supported demand response (DR) in IES. The proposed model connects day-ahead flexibility clearing, multi-storage scheduling, learning-based decision support, real-time capability assessment, safety-filtered recourse, and verified service delivery within a unified hierarchical structure. In the day-ahead stage, a leader–follower market mechanism clears storage-supported load-to-grid commitments while considering distribution feasibility, settlement consistency, scenario-based risk exposure, and available storage capability. At the integrated energy system level, heterogeneous storage assets, conversion units, and comfort-aware flexible loads are coordinated to transform cleared commitments into device-feasible multi-carrier schedules. A constrained deep reinforcement learning (DRL) mechanism is used to solve the high-dimensional scheduling problem, while large language model (LLM) assistance is restricted to bounded reward calibration and storage-capability-aware repair-template selection rather than direct dispatch. During real-time execution, the cleared schedule is lifted into a fast delivery layer in which disturbance-aware estimation, storage-aware safety filtering, corrective recourse, fallback switching, and service verification determine whether the committed flexibility can be delivered, partially restored, or conservatively degraded. The framework therefore treats storage-supported DR not as a static cleared quantity, but as a physically constrained service whose credibility must be maintained from market commitment to real-time delivery. Numerical results demonstrate coherent scalability across benchmark, real-world, and large-scale systems, preserved storage-supported operational headroom, real-time delivery above 88% under compound disturbances, and bounded constraint excursions below 3%. Ablation, stability, sensitivity, and comparative analyses confirm that performance gains arise from the integrated storage-supported resilience chain rather than from isolated scheduling or control components.

title: Reliability and Effectiveness of Autonomous AI Agents in Supply Chain Management
affiliations: , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - School of Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), Harvard University - John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Georgia Institute of Technology - Operations Management Area and Harvard University

detail.title: Reliability and Effectiveness of Autonomous AI Agents in Supply Chain Management
detail.abstract: This paper studies autonomous generative AI agents in multi-echelon supply chains using the MIT Beer Game. We identify four inference-time levers that shape performance: model selection, policies and guardrails, centralized data sharing, and prompt engineering. Model capability is the dominant factor: an out-of-the-box reasoning model exceeds human-level performance, and optimized reasoning models reduce costs by up to 67% relative to human teams. However, strong average performance masks substantial reliability risks. We introduce the agent bullwhip, the amplification of decision unreliability across echelons, manifesting along two dimensions: decision variance increases both across facilities at the same point in time and within the same facility across time. We develop a mathematical framework showing that this phenomenon is inherent to multi-agent systems that involve coordination and information delays, and we demonstrate that repeated sampling fails to meaningfully reduce it. To address this limitation, we propose a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)-based reinforcement-learning post-training framework that trains a shared base LLM using system-level supply-chain rewards. GRPO post-training substantially reduces tail events, curtails agent bullwhip, and improves the reliability of autonomous supply-chain agents.

title: Provider-Dependent Behavioral Asymmetries in LLM Trading Agents: Evidence from the Brazilian Equity Market

detail.title: Provider-Dependent Behavioral Asymmetries in LLM Trading Agents: Evidence from the Brazilian Equity Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available financial market data and does not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was developed independently by the author as an academic extension of a course project.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit behavioral asymmetries analogous to those predicted by Prospect Theory (PT) when deployed as decision-making agents in an equity trading context. Using a hybrid quantitative-LLM agent architecture applied to Brazilian equity assets (B3 exchange) over a 730-day period (April 2024-April 2026), we test three behavioral hypotheses across three distinct model providers: GPT-5.4 (OpenAI), Claude Haiku (Anthropic), and Qwen-8B (local, via LM Studio). To enable an apples-to-apples comparison, all cross-provider statistics are computed on a common 5-asset core subset (ABEV3, ITUB4, PETR4, VALE3, WEGE3); a 23-asset full-universe run is retained for Qwen-8B as a robustness check. We find consistent evidence for frequency asymmetry (H2b): all three providers emit significantly more long than short signals on the matched subset (L/S ratios: 1.26×, 5.94×, and 10.47×, respectively; χ 2 p < 0.001 in all cases). Critically, the magnitude of this asymmetry varies by nearly an order of magnitude across architectures, suggesting that provider-specific training and model scale shape decision behavior more than any universal behavioral tendency. Confidence asymmetry (H2a) is inconclusive or reversed across providers, and neutrality-under-volatility (H2c) is consistently refuted: all three agents become more active under high-volatility regimes, contradicting PT's ambiguity-aversion prediction. Expressed confidence is poorly calibrated (ECE: 0.17-0.29) and non-informative as a signal filter across all providers. These results have practical implications for practitioners who deploy LLMbased trading signals, and raise important questions about whether observed behavioral asymmetries in LLMs primarily reflect internalized human heuristics or are artifacts of training corpus, model scale, and alignment procedures.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence systems generate durable competitive advantage not through any single output but through the learning that accumulates across training, fine-tuning, and deployment. Model weights, embeddings, and internal parameter updates encode this learning, yet they fall outside the scope of copyright’s derivative works doctrine because they are functional, not expressive. Copyright law’s exclusion of systems and processes from protection is not an oversight; it is a deliberate boundary. But that boundary has not prevented the allocation of exclusive control over AI learning. It has merely shifted the site of allocation from statute to contract.  

This Essay identifies and names a phenomenon it calls contractual derivatives: learning-based assets that are not statutory derivative works but are rendered proprietary through private ordering. Through service framing, narrow output definitions, residual rights clauses, improvement provisions, and use restrictions, AI vendors have constructed contractual architectures that replicate the exclusionary effects of intellectual property without invoking its doctrines. The Essay argues that these arrangements raise concerns at the intersection of copyright preemption, consent theory, and competition.

title: The Missing Modality: Regulatory Architecture, Epistemic Failure, and the Political Economy of Ghana's Cocoa Crisis

detail.title: The Missing Modality: Regulatory Architecture, Epistemic Failure, and the Political Economy of Ghana's Cocoa Crisis
detail.abstract: This article reframes Ghana's 2025/26 cocoa sector crisis-conventionally interpreted as a commodity price shock-as the systemic output of a regulatory architecture in which three of Lessig's four modalities of governance operate while the fourth is underdeveloped relative to the regulatory obligations it must support. Law, market incentives, and social norms are present. What is underdeveloped is the technological regulatory infrastructure that makes legal mandates consistently enforceable, market signals epistemically reliable, and governance norms disciplined by verifiable accountability. The 2023/24 production forecast deviationwhich triggered US$1.3 billion in forward contract losses-was not primarily a forecasting error but an epistemic failure: the institution produced a projection on data structurally incapable of reflecting ground-truth conditions. Drawing on Lessig's modalities framework, Lipsky's street-level bureaucracy theory, Deming and Juran's quality systems theory, and Wang and Strong's information quality framework, the article argues that structural reform requires 2 not additional legislation-laws already exist-but technological regulatory infrastructure through which those laws apply completely and consistently-capable of surfacing patterns of selective enforcement and rent-seeking where they occur. The fourth modality's underdevelopment is not explained by resource constraint: it has served those who benefit from regulatory gaps at the expense of the farmers the framework is designed to protect.

title: Border Effects in Social Connectedness

detail.title: Border Effects in Social Connectedness
detail.abstract: I examine the effect of state borders on social connectedness using a gravity framework applied to U.S. county-to-county Facebook friendship data. I find that crossing a state border reduces social connectedness by approximately 62%, even after controlling for geographic distance and contiguity, consistent with (Bailey, Cao, Kuchler, Stroebel, & Wong, 2018). I test four mechanisms: average undergraduate enrollment, flagship university (tested through host-county presence, shared catchment area, and own catchment area), shared commuting zones, and political differences. Counties hosting a flagship and those with higher enrollment exhibit weaker within-state ties, consistent with a national orientation effect. Counties within a flagship's catchment area show stronger within-state ties, consistent with a meeting-place effect, suggesting that proximity to a flagship strengthens home bias even as hosting one weakens it. Shared commuting zones emerge as the strongest mechanism-within-state pairs sharing a local economic community show significantly stronger social ties, consistent with local economic integration reinforcing home bias. Political dissimilarity reduces social connectedness, independent of the border, and amplifies the cross-border penalty. Despite these findings, the border effect remains large and significant across all specifications, suggesting that additional sources of border friction remain unidentified

title: Sovereignty by Design: A Northeast Asian Union and the Fourth Polity

detail.title: Sovereignty by Design: A Northeast Asian Union and the Fourth Polity
detail.abstract: This essay argues that meaningful Northeast Asian regional integration-and with it durable regional peace and deeper economic cooperation-is achievable, but only if all four polities of any future framework, China, Japan, South Korea, and any northern Korean entity, develop a common vocabulary for pooling comparable elements of their sovereignty in roughly equivalent terms. The substantive requirement is symmetric, but the design opportunities are not. The central claim is that the constitutional moment of a meaningful DPRK transformation, in whatever form it eventually takes, is the rare circumstance in which one of the four contributions to the framework can be designed at founding rather than retrofitted against existing legal inertia (Benelux Union, n.d.; Austrian State Treaty, 1955). The other three contributions must be assembled out of inherited constitutional and alliance architecture; the fourth alone can be purpose-built. The argument begins from an ASEAN-centered perspective developed in earlier work on Southeast Asian regionalism and proceeds through a reconsideration of what statehood itself means in an era when every functioning state already pools elements of its sovereignty. In this view, the question facing Northeast Asia is not whether any single polity can be safely absorbed or transformed but whether all four can together accept the reciprocal pooling on which serious regional architecture, regional peace, and the next stage of economic cooperation all depend. The intra-Korean questions of reunification, federation, and absorption-important in their own right-are treated here only insofar as they bear on this regional framework, and are properly the subject of separate inquiry.

detail.abstract:
This Article examines whether competition enforcement can meaningfully address wealth inequality in the digital economy, and identifies a critical precondition for its legitimacy: institutional independence. Drawing on landmark enforcement actions across EU, UK, and US jurisdictions, we argue that antitrust occupies a vital secondary role in mitigating inequality—complementing tax policy, labor law, and social programs—when properly insulated from geopolitical capture.

The Article proceeds in three parts. First, we analyze how dominant digital platforms generate wealth concentration through self-preferencing (Google Shopping, Case AT.39740, €2.42 billion fine, upheld by the CJEU in September 2024), tying and exclusivity (Google Android, Case AT.40099; Microsoft, Case T-201/04), and exploitative data practices (Meta v Bundeskartellamt, confirmed in CJEU Case C-252/21). The €465 million Idealo damages award in November 2025 illustrates competition enforcement's growing capacity to recapture wealth flowing from competitors and consumers to platform shareholders. Second, we examine labor market antitrust through the High-Tech Employee Antitrust Litigation and the DOJ's evolving criminal enforcement program, demonstrating how antitrust prevents coordinated wage suppression. Third, we explore the accommodation of sustainability objectives under Chapter 9 of the 2023 EU Horizontal Cooperation Guidelines.

The Article concludes with a cautionary analysis of competition law's geopolitical instrumentalization, contrasting the European Competition Network's principled response to the Ukraine crisis with Russia's coercive deployment of antitrust institutions to compel continued market presence by foreign undertakings. We argue that competition law's contribution to addressing inequality requires preserving institutional independence, procedural fairness, and the rule of law.

title: Representative Equivalence and Hetero Behaviorus Economies (When Homo Economicus Aggregation Fails)

detail.title: Representative Equivalence and Hetero Behaviorus Economies (When Homo Economicus Aggregation Fails)
detail.abstract: Representative-agent reductions are central to dynamic macroeconomic analysis. This paper provides a necessary and sufficient characterization of when such reductions are valid in economies with heterogeneous decision architectures. Within a general equilibrium framework with a measurable type space, we show that representative equivalence holds if and only if aggregate actions are invariant to all economically admissible type distributions. This occurs precisely when the family of individual decision mappings collapses almost everywhere. When this condition fails, equilibrium dynamics depend on the distribution of types as a state variable; we refer to such environments as Hetero Behaviorus economies. We then analyze the dynamic implications of distribution-dependent aggregation. The equilibrium transition operator forms a family indexed by the type distribution, and local stability is governed by the associated Jacobians. Although each pure-type economy may be locally stable, convex combinations of type-specific Jacobians can generate instability. We provide explicit composition-induced bifurcation results and characterize distributionuniform stability using spectral bounds over the convex hull of admissible linearizations. Trace-determinant conditions yield sharp boundaries in low dimension, while spectral hull conditions provide dimension-free stability criteria. The results establish that heterogeneity in decision architecture is structurally consequential precisely when it affects aggregation, and that distributional composition alone can alter stability properties even when fundamentals remain fixed. These conditions carry empirical content: representative equivalence is a testable restriction on the observable distribution of decision architectures, and its failure is directly detectable in environments with heterogeneous expectations where belief dispersion is measurable.

title: What Counts as a Psychedelic?

detail.title: What Counts as a Psychedelic?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The term “psychedelic” lacks a consensus definition, yet a growing body of regulatory and commercial infrastructure—FDA clinical-trial guidance, AMA reimbursement codes, research grants, and insurance coverage decisions—turns on whether a given substance falls within the category. This short essay argues that the boundaries of the “psychedelic” label are doing significant normative work that is too often left unexamined. While LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, MDMA, and ketamine are commonly included, structurally similar substances such as PCP, methamphetamine, and diphenhydramine are routinely excluded—not because of meaningful pharmacological distinctions, but because their reputations would tarnish the “psychedelic” brand. The essay traces the etymology of the term, examines its “classical” pharmacological criteria, and shows how the current categorization risks perpetuating forms of drug elitism with classist and racist antecedents (recalling the crack-versus-cocaine sentencing disparity). It calls on academics, regulators, and industry actors to pre-establish and publicly articulate the criteria by which a substance qualifies as “psychedelic,” so that those criteria can be subjected to critique and refinement.

AI as Institutional Amplifier -A Field Research Case Study

detail.title:
The Weighted Mirror 
AI as Institutional Amplifier -A Field Research Case Study
detail.abstract: AI is a mirror and an amplifier of its creators. The institutions building it tried to make the machine more human while demonstrating a lack of humanity toward the people it was built for. The field exists to sustain the field. The everyday person was the stated beneficiary and the absent variable. This is not an argument that AI is dangerous. It is an argument that neutral tools built by non-neutral humans produce weighted outputs-and that the weight goes unacknowledged at every layer of the process.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a decentralized governance framework termed the Village Parishad Model, designed to address inefficiencies in existing rural and urban administrative systems in India. The model integrates immediate service delivery, functional decentralization through sectoral responsibility assignments, production-linked rural economies, and a post-audit accountability mechanism. The framework emphasizes eliminating administrative delays, reducing financial leakage, and ensuring direct citizen-centered governance. It further suggests integrating rural production systems with state-supported procurement and profit-sharing mechanisms to enhance local economic sustainability. The study argues that such a model can significantly improve rural service delivery efficiency, reduce migration pressures, and strengthen grassroots democracy.

title:
Performance Measure Calibration in Workforce Reemployment Programs: 
A Methodological Assessment of the Texas 10-Week Reemployment Threshold
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
Performance Measure Calibration in Workforce Reemployment Programs: 
A Methodological Assessment of the Texas 10-Week Reemployment Threshold
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the Texas Workforce Commission's (TWC) Claimant Reemployment within 10 Weeks local Workforce Development Board performance measure reflects observed Texas unemployment insurance (UI) claimant flow. Using annual data published in U.S. Department of Labor Employment and Training Administration Handbook 394 for the period 2008 through 2024, I apply the duration-decomposition identity—average claim duration is the exhaustion-weighted average of exhaustee duration and non-exhauster duration—to recover the implied average duration of claimants who exit the UI rolls before reaching the 26-week regular-benefit cap. The implied non-exhauster duration falls below the 10-week threshold in only one of the seventeen years examined (2008). The recent series, including the post-COVID labor market trough of 2022, prints between 10.6 and 10.9 weeks. The federal RESEA performance gate established by the U.S. Department of Labor for fiscal year 2022 is set at 15 weeks—five weeks longer than the Texas local Board threshold—and is consistent with observed Texas average duration. The paper documents a substantial gap between the threshold imposed at the local Board level and the duration distribution of the targeted population, and treats the question of how the 10-week figure was originally calibrated as an empirical question deserving further investigation. The paper's contribution is methodological: a duration-decomposition framework that uses publicly available annual Handbook 394 data to test the consistency of fixed-numeric reemployment thresholds against the underlying UI flow.

title: Bridging the Silos in Affective AI: A Critical Perspective from Data to Society
affiliations: Kansai University

detail.title: Bridging the Silos in Affective AI: A Critical Perspective from Data to Society
detail.abstract: Affective computing has grown into a field that spans emotion theory, multimodal data, computational modeling, human-AI interaction, social applications, and ethical evaluation, yet most existing surveys address only one or two of these layers at a time and fail to capture how the layers depend on one another. Rather than offering another comprehensive survey, this position paper reorganizes the field around a six-layer pipeline and reads the literature as a chain of dependencies in which upstream design choices propagate into downstream evaluation, deployment, and governance. Our central diagnosis is that four \emph{silo-bridge patterns} recur across the field: disconnections at the theory/data (Pattern~1), modeling/interaction (Pattern~2), technology/ethics (Pattern~3), and data/social-application (Pattern~4) boundaries. These are not incidental implementation problems but recurring failure modes rooted in the pipeline structure itself, forming a cascade in which upstream patterns structurally enable downstream ones. As a prescriptive program, we present five integrated design criteria: theory-explicit affective representation (DC1), affective reasoning with bounded intervention (DC2), longitudinal interaction-in-the-loop evaluation (DC3), deployment-specific affective accountability (DC4), and user-retained interpretive authority (DC5). The five criteria are designed as an interlocking response to the cascade rather than as independent recommendations. We situate affective AI not as a mere recognition or generation technology but as a sociotechnical system that can intervene in human emotional interpretation, interaction, and social decision-making, and call upon future research to move toward systems that are more coherent, more responsible, and more respectful of human emotional agency.

title: FedCAFE: A Federated Cross-Attention Feature Exchange Framework for Heterogeneous Large Language Model Fine-tuning
affiliations: Zhengzhou University, Zhejiang Lab and Anhui University of Science and Technology

detail.title: FedCAFE: A Federated Cross-Attention Feature Exchange Framework for Heterogeneous Large Language Model Fine-tuning
detail.abstract: Federated learning provides an effective paradigm for privacy-preserving collaborative fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs). In practical deployments, however, servers and clients constrained by device resources often hold pre-trained models heterogeneous in both parameter scale and archi tecture, while most existing federated LLM fine-tuning frameworks adopt homogeneous aggregation methods such as FedAvg, which are inapplicable to such heterogeneous scenarios. How to effectively f ine-tune a server-side large model using heterogeneous small client models therefore becomes a key challenge. To this end, we propose FedCAFE, a bidirectional feature-level alignment framework for heterogeneous federated LLM fine-tuning. FedCAFE designs two complementary cross-attention adapters — the Up-Adapter and Down-Adapter — to respectively translate feature spaces from small client models to the large server model and vice versa, together with a four-phase training pipeline that employs composite adapter loss training and selective distillation to achieve effective knowledge transfer, thereby improving both server-side and client-side model performance. Experiments on multiple QA benchmarks demonstrate that FedCAFE can effectively fine-tune the server-side large model by leveraging heterogeneous small client models, yielding performance improvements.

title: FiCoTS: Fine-to-Coarse LLM-Enhanced Hierarchical Cross-Modality Interaction for Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Great Bay University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: FiCoTS: Fine-to-Coarse LLM-Enhanced Hierarchical Cross-Modality Interaction for Time Series Forecasting
detail.abstract: The recent success of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers significant potential for time series forecasting, particularly in cross-modality setting. The prevailing LLM-as-Predictor paradigm uses LLM as the forecasting backbone, but the semantic gap between text and time series hinders LLM from adequately understanding time series. Alternatively, LLM-as-Enhancer paradigm employs LLM only to encode text as complementary information. However, existing LLM-as-Enhancer methods typically perform shallow, coarse-grained cross-modality interaction, overlooking the underlying semantic discrepancy. To address this challenge, we propose FiCoTS, an LLM-enhanced fine-to-coarse framework for multimodal time series forecasting. FiCoTS facilitates progressive cross-modality interaction at three semantic levels in a fine-to-coarse scheme. First, in the token-level modality alignment module, a dynamic heterogeneous graph is constructed to filter noise and align time series patches with text tokens. Second, in the feature-level modality interaction module, a global cross-attention mechanism is introduced to enable each time series variable to connect with relevant textual contexts. Third, in the decision-level modality fusion module, a gated network is designed to adaptively fuse the results of the two modalities for robust predictions. Extensive experiments on seven real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, especially in few-shot scenarios. The codes will be released.

title: Comparison of Geothermal Power to Solar Photovoltaic Power in Oman as a Viable Renewable Energy Source
affiliations: University of Buraimi

detail.title: Comparison of Geothermal Power to Solar Photovoltaic Power in Oman as a Viable Renewable Energy Source

publicationDetails.detailsText: Osama A. Marzouk (2026). Comparison of geothermal power to solar photovoltaic power in Oman as a viable renewable energy source. Cleaner Energy Systems. volume 13, article 100257.

detail.abstract: The Sultanate of Oman enjoys plenty of solar energy and wind energy; both have been exploited successfully in the country. However, geothermal energy has not been exploited yet in Oman. This natural heat source deserves more studies to assess its technical potential and economic feasibility compared to other electricity generation technologies in Oman. The current study fills this gap by presenting a techno-economic assessment (TEA) of a small 30-MW geothermal power plant in Oman, operating on a binary (two-fluid) cycle, with a drilling depth of 2 km. The analysis was performed using the renowned software tool SAM (System Advisor Model) of the United States National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL). The current results suggest a levelized cost of energy (LCOE) of 8.68 cents/kWh (0.0868 US$/kWh) or 33.4 baisa/kWh (0.0334 OMR/kWh). When compared with electricity tariff or solar photovoltaic (PV) power purchase agreement (PPA) rates in Oman, it was found that geothermal-based electricity is too expensive. Furthermore, the estimated geothermal LCOE is more than three times the LCOE value of self-owned photovoltaic (PV) power systems in Oman, which is around 10 baisa/kWh (0.010 OMR/kWh). The estimated first-year electricity generation for the geothermal power plant model is 261.268 GWh/year, leading to a specific electricity generation of 8709 kWh/kW/year. This is about five times the specific power generation from PV power plants. The study is augmented by sensitivity analyses and regression models to help understand the impact of multiple input parameters. The study provides novel results regarding decision-making for geothermal power investment in Oman.

title: Data-Driven Platform of Platforms to Drive Business and ESG Practices in Decentralized Supply Chains

detail.title: Data-Driven Platform of Platforms to Drive Business and ESG Practices in Decentralized Supply Chains
detail.abstract: In the digital era, the adoption of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) standards is increasingly prioritized by companies, particularly within decentralized supply chains. With ESG investments projected to reach US$53 trillion by 2025, there is growing pressure for sustainable business practices. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in logistics and mobility sectors face barriers in accessing capital and implementing ESG practices due to fragmented data systems and lack of transparency. This research introduces a Data-Driven Platform of Platforms (DPoP) model that integrates stakeholders across decentralized supply chains, enhancing collaboration, transparency, and ESG adoption through data sharing and network effects. The findings indicate that the DPoP model enhances both absorptive capacity and institutional compliance, leading to improved ESG practices, cost efficiency, and data-driven decision-making. This research advances the field by integrating absorptive capacity with institutional compliance, providing a scalable DPoP model that empowers SMEs to leverage ESG opportunities, thus driving sustainable growth and industry innovation.

title: The Architecture of the Business Cycle: A Multi-Object, Multi-Country, Forward-Looking Operator Framework with an Application to the Postwar Macroeconomic Record

detail.title: The Architecture of the Business Cycle: A Multi-Object, Multi-Country, Forward-Looking Operator Framework with an Application to the Postwar Macroeconomic Record
detail.abstract: The macroeconomics literature contains rival accounts of the business cycle-real, monetary, financial, news, uncertainty, international-that have coexisted for two decades because each describes a different layer of a coupled dynamic system whose univariate projection is observed output. The scalar question "what drives the business cycle" is mis-specified when the underlying phenomenon is a projection of a layered state vector. This paper develops the architecture that the question requires. Each macroeconomic object (output, prices, labor, credit, asset prices, exchange rate, expectations) is represented by a local layered system with activation, transition, and readout matrices. Objects couple within a country through a within-country coupling matrix C and across countries through same-object coupling D and cross-object spillover E. Lags enter through state augmentation; forward-looking beliefs enter through a structural belief law whose projection onto observed coordinates is the operator law Φ. Four theorems characterize the framework: a layered decomposition theorem that uniquely attributes any movement in the global readout to an origin country, origin object, and activation layer; a joint reachability theorem that defines when a policy instrument can stabilize an unstable mode of the global system; a forward-looking operator-law recovery proposition that identifies the operator law up to a Lucas-equivalence class; and a lag-expectation equivalence theorem that formalizes the observational equivalence of long memory and forward-looking beliefs absent identifying restrictions. The framework is implemented on a quarterly panel of five major economies (United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan) from 1955 to 2026 using publicly available data, with operator-state coordinates estimated by rolling local projections and a belief state extracted as a principal component of survey and market-based expectations indicators. The empirical implementation documents three results that no single-layer framework can produce. First, the within-country price-on-price coupling for the United States moves from −0.01 during the Global Financial Crisis and zero-lower-bound regime to +1.46 in the post-COVID regime — a movement that is the architectural signature of Φ-reactivation rather than a slope change. Second, the policy reachability of the operator block, measured by the minimum singular value of the controllability matrix, deteriorates by an order of magnitude between the post-2008 regime (2.5 × 10−4 ) and the post-COVID regime (1.9 × 10−3 ), with the GFC regime being the empirical case of the unreachable-mode condition. Third, layer attribution of the 2008 and 2020 recessions produces distinct architectural signatures: the 2008 episode loads on financial and monetary coordinates with substantial cross-country dispersion, while the 2020 episode loads almost exclusively on the monetary coordinate with synchronized signs across all five economies. The framework reduces the major business-cycle traditions to special cases of a single coupled architecture and re-reads thirty years of policy debate as a sequence of layer-localization errors. The implication for policy is the replacement of (π, x)-space Taylor rules and inflation-targeting frameworks with operator-coordinate feedback rules in the global state, the recognition of communication as a Φ-instrument, the reassignment of institutional responsibility by layer, and the redefinition of international coordination as joint reachability rather than rate harmonization. The paper closes by stating the research program this implies: the systematic re-examination of macroeconomic primitives that are scalar projections of layered systems — the natural rate of interest, the equity premium, exchange-rate disconnect, and growth divergence are immediate candidates — each waiting for the same architectural operation.

title: Representative Seasonal Time-Window Sampling of Residential Energy Consumption Using Evolutionary AI and DTW Optimization
affiliations: Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology, Ewha Womans University, Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology and Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology

detail.title: Representative Seasonal Time-Window Sampling of Residential Energy Consumption Using Evolutionary AI and DTW Optimization
detail.abstract: In large-scale residential field studies, long-term monitoring can provide strong representativeness, but it is not always practical under constraints such as cost, equipment operation, data-quality control, and repeated site visits. This study addresses that gap by presenting a field-oriented framework for deriving representative seasonal monitoring windows that preserve annual representativeness while remaining practically deployable. Using one year of hourly heating, cooling, and lighting data from 60 apartment households in Seoul, South Korea (8,760 h; approximately 1.5 million end-use-specific observations), representative-window selection was formulated as a large-scale continuous-interval search problem in which both start timing and duration vary simultaneously. Candidate windows were encoded as chromosomes and explored through an evolutionary AI framework built on a genetic algorithm (GA), while household-specific seasonal reference profiles were matched using dynamic time warping (DTW), thereby making an otherwise computationally prohibitive search operationally tractable. The retained household-level candidate pools showed a median similarity of 0.89, indicating strong profile preservation at the dwelling level. These household-level candidates were then synthesized along the seasonal calendar into integrated 28-day monitoring windows for each season and end use. The resulting integrated windows achieved 77-97% household coverage across seasons and end uses, while cross-end-use temporal overlaps also indicated the feasibility of co-scheduled monitoring. Overall, the proposed framework translates household-level representativeness into deployable field schedules, providing a practical basis for reducing monitoring time and cost without materially compromising annual representativeness in residential energy studies.

title: What Derives Firms Valuation in GCC? An Panel ARDL Analysis of P/E Ratio Determinats
affiliations: Higher College of Technology, Higher College of Technology,  and Higher College of Technology

detail.title: What Derives Firms Valuation in GCC? An Panel ARDL Analysis of P/E Ratio Determinats
detail.abstract: The paper explores the impact of short-and long-term financial ratios on price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios in the GCC countries from first quarter of 2012 to the fourth quarter of 2022. The study employs the panel Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) approach to estimate both shortrun and long-run relationships among the variables. The long-run results reveal that sales per share and book value per share significantly affect the P/E ratio, while earnings per share (EPS) exert the strongest influence among all explanatory variables. In contrast, dividends per share and cash flow per share show relatively weaker effects. The short-run findings further confirm the presence of a long-term equilibrium relationship among the variables included in the model. Given that the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio serves as a cornerstone of firm valuation and investment strategy, uncovering its financial determinants is imperative for GCC economies pursuing strategic income diversification. The findings provide useful implications for policymakers by highlighting the importance of financial ratios in shaping investor behavior and supporting financial stability policies. The results indicate that investors may benefit from focusing on firms with strong earnings per share performance.

title: Retail Option Imbalance and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns

detail.title: Retail Option Imbalance and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
detail.abstract: I document that retail option-trade imbalances predict the cross-section of U.S. stock returns. Sorting stocks daily into deciles by call-side single-leg-auction (SLIM) imbalance [Bryzgalova et al., 2023] generates a long-short portfolio that earns +25.75 basis points per day (t = 2.26, annualized Sharpe ratio 1.76) over November 2019 to June 2021. The Fama-French six-factor alpha is +26.82 bps (t = 2.52), with a significantly negative market beta (-0.34) and negative momentum loading (-0.21): risk factors absorb essentially none of the spread. The signal is positive in both the retail-trading boom of March 2020-March 2021 and in the surrounding period (+33.16 bps, t = 2.61), and survives the exclusion of meme tickers (post-exclusion t = 1.84, down only 18%). The cumulative long-short return peaks at horizon h = 2 trading days (+61.77 bps, t = 2.50) and then declines monotonically, consistent with an overshooting-correction pattern rather than either pure continuation or rapid mean reversion. These findings are inconsistent with the view that retail option flow is uninformative noise, and motivate a richer test in the post-2022 daily-expiration regime, where the maturity dimension can adjudicate among information-based, gamma-hedging, and lottery-driven mechanisms.

title: Effects of spent mushroom substrate and vermicompost on organic matter dynamics in highly weathered soil
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Wageningen University & Research and Wageningen University

detail.title: Effects of spent mushroom substrate and vermicompost on organic matter dynamics in highly weathered soil
detail.abstract: Soil organic matter (SOM) is vital for soil health and agricultural productivity, especially in the highly weathered soils of Sub-Saharan Africa. Effective crop residue management is crucial for replenishing SOM. Circular residue use for oyster mushroom cultivation and subsequent vermiculture holds considerable potential for enhancing food security in the region. However, the effects of the resulting organic amendments on SOM dynamics remain unclear compared to traditional practices like residue removal, mulching, and burning. Here we study the impact of five maize stover-derived amendments on SOM dynamics in highly weathered soil. Treatments included unprocessed stover, burned stover, spent oyster mushroom substrate, and two vermicomposts, applied at rates reflecting processing losses from equivalent stover yields. Over a 51-day incubation, heterotrophic respiration was monitored to assess microbial activity. At the end of the experiment, microbial biomass was analysed using phospholipid fatty acids, and SOM fractions were assessed through a density-based approach. Results showed that all amendments, except burned stover, significantly influenced SOM dynamics. Unprocessed maize stover application resulted in the highest microbial activity and biomass compared with processed amendments. Despite varying carbon inputs, soil carbon stocks remained unchanged relative to the control. Nonetheless, the relative contribution of particulate organic matter (POM) compared with the mineral-associated matter (MAOM) fraction increased in processed amendments. The degree of processing influenced SOM formation pathways, with potential long-term implications for soil functioning. Our results show that in the short term, circular crop residue use has the potential to preserve soil carbon while producing high-quality protein, contributing to local food security.

title: When Does Bad News Stick? Topic-Level Asymmetry in Narrative Dynamics
affiliations: , University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business and Cornell University - Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management

detail.title: When Does Bad News Stick? Topic-Level Asymmetry in Narrative Dynamics
detail.abstract: When does bad news stick? This paper shows that the persistence of media sentiment depends not only on whether news is good or bad, but also on what the news is about. Using the complete Wall Street Journal archive from 1990 to 2025, we construct monthly positive and negative sentiment indices for twelve economic topics and estimate topic-specific sentiment dynamics. Bad-news innovations generate larger cumulative responses than positive-news innovations in every topic, indicating that negativity asymmetry is a broad feature of media sentiment. But the size of this asymmetry varies sharply across topics. The bad-minus-good persistence gap is largest in security and human rights, health and public safety, real estate and financial stability, and firms and corporate strategy. Bad-news persistence is also sizable in data-rich topics such as financial markets, real estate, and corporate news, suggesting that frequent information arrival does not necessarily lead narratives to revert quickly. These findings show that aggregate sentiment indices mask substantial topic-level heterogeneity in the asymmetric dynamics of narratives, with potential implications for how persistent negative sentiment shapes expectations, asset prices, and real economic outcomes.

title: Do GDP-Linked Bonds Reduce Extreme Public Debt Risk? Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa *
affiliations: University of Orleans - Laboratoire d'économie d'Orléans

detail.title: Do GDP-Linked Bonds Reduce Extreme Public Debt Risk? Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa *
detail.abstract: This paper assesses, under empirically grounded macroeconomic conditions, whether GDP-linked bonds can meaningfully reduce extreme public debt outcomes in Sub-Saharan African economies, where volatility, fiscal dominance, and market incompleteness are structurally more pronounced than in advanced economies. Using a panel of 15 countries, we show that, although the magnitude of the gains depends on the indexation formula, GDPlinked bonds significantly compress the upper tail of the public-debt distribution, leading to sizable reductions at the 99th percentile under severe macroeconomic shocks. These results remain robust, as GDP-linked bonds outperform conventional bonds even when risk premia of 100 and 200 basis points are applied. We further compare two alternative indexation schemes-coupon-indexed bonds and nominally indexed bonds-and find that coupon indexation delivers systematically larger stabilizing gains. Finally, we propose a theoretical framework to price GDP-linked bonds and derive their risk premia, explicitly incorporating uncertainty risks faced by issuing countries. Taken together, this paper does not seek to re-establish the theoretical case for GDP-linked bonds, but rather to clarify the macro-financial conditions under which such instruments can meaningfully enhance sovereign debt resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: The Finance Researcher’s Favorite – President Donald Trump and the Stock Market
affiliations: Technical University of Darmstadt, Technical University of Darmstadt and Technical University of Darmstadt

detail.title: The Finance Researcher’s Favorite – President Donald Trump and the Stock Market
detail.abstract: No other politician has stood in the spotlight of financial analyses as frequently as U.S. President Donald Trump. Such attention appears appropriate only if the individual succeeds in consistently influencing the pricing of financial markets. This study systematically reviews and synthesizes the empirical findings regarding the stock market effects of Donald Trump. Drawing on a Web of Science search and applying inclusion criteria, 57 peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 2025 are identified and analyzed along four thematic dimensions: overall market and index reactions, sectoral differences, political communication, and international spillovers. The synthesis shows that Trump’s elections trigger positive short-term index returns alongside pronounced spikes in implied volatility. At the sectoral level, financials, industrials, and growth-sensitive industries emerge as consistent winners, whereas health care and defensive sectors decline. Brown assets temporarily benefit from anticipated deregulation, while green assets lose value in the short run, though firms with strong climate commitments and long-run investor horizons earn positive returns. President Trump’s tweets generate short-lived yet robust effects on trading volume and volatility, while return responses vary with sentiment, data frequency, and tweet topic, particularly for trade and monetary-policy-related statements.

title: IMU-Aided Wireless Positioning Compensation for Robust Indoor Localization During Outages
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Research Institute of Highway Ministry of Transport, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

detail.title: IMU-Aided Wireless Positioning Compensation for Robust Indoor Localization During Outages
detail.abstract: Accurate indoor localization is an important requirement in modern society. The fusion of ultrawideband (UWB) and inertial navigation is a commonly used positioning strategy. However, in complex environments, UWB observations may be blocked by obstacles or degraded by multipath, causing UWB outages and leaving the accumulated error of inertial navigation insufficiently constrained. To address this problem, this paper proposes an inertial-guidance-assisted UWB outage compensation algorithm based on a self-attention gated recurrent unit (SAT-GRU). The main innovation is to reformulate UWB outage compensation as a navigation-frame UWB position-increment prediction problem rather than direct absolute-position prediction or generic INS error regression. When UWB signals are available, IMU measurements together with extrapolated velocity and attitude are used to learn the temporal mapping to UWB position increments. When UWB signals are missing, the trained SAT-GRU adaptively weights informative motion segments in the IMU sequence and outputs pseudo-UWB increments for fusion localization. Field tests show that the proposed algorithm achieves a 68.75% improvement over pure inertial navigation, a 54.5% improvement over LSTM-based prediction, and a 64.3% improvement over GRU-based prediction, demonstrating the effectiveness and engineering applicability of the proposed method.

title: Bargaining Space Does Not Always Exist: A Formal Refutation of Fearon's Foundational Assumption and the Impossibility of Perpetual Peace

detail.title: Bargaining Space Does Not Always Exist: A Formal Refutation of Fearon's Foundational Assumption and the Impossibility of Perpetual Peace
detail.abstract: James Fearon's "Rationalist Explanations for War" (1995) rests on the foundational claim that a bargaining range always exists between rational actors, since war is costly for both sides and its costs can always be avoided through negotiated settlement. This paper mounts a three-part challenge to that claim. First, using Fearon's own mathematical framework, we show that once the winner's ex post value is permitted to exceed the pre-war value of the contested good — because certain goods are structurally inaccessible through consensual bargaining — the bargaining range disappears under a precise, falsifiable threshold condition. Second, we introduce a dynamic extension showing that even where bargaining space exists initially, repeated coercive interaction erodes it through endogenous value transfer, generating an irreversibility threshold beyond which no negotiated settlement can exist. Third, we model conflict between dyadic pairs as a non-stationary Markov chain with war as an absorbing state, whose transition probabilities drift systematically toward absorption as a function of cumulative coercive history. Under multiplicity of armed agents (N ≥ 2) and sufficient time, the probability that at least one dyadic pair reaches the absorbing war state approaches unity. We conclude that perpetual peace is not merely unlikely but probabilistically excluded given multiple armed agents. Peace-maintaining mechanisms — democratic governance, economic interdependence, diplomacy, cultural exchange — function in our framework by slowing the rate of escalation drift, not by eliminating it. They constitute procrastination of absorption, not its negation. This result formalises, within a rational-choice framework, the realist intuition that war is a permanent condition of international life. We further show that balance-of-power, bipolar stability, multipolar equilibrium, and regional concert theories are formally recast as theories of escalation procrastination rather than peace: they extend the expected time to absorption but do not eliminate the positive drift toward it. The two structural escape conditions our model admits — hegemonic monopoly on armed force (N = 1) and universal disarmament (N = 0) — connect the argument to the tradition of world government theory, deriving this conclusion not from ethical idealism but from the internal logic of the rationalist bargaining framework itself. We position the paper against Fearon (1995), Powell (1999, 2002), Slantchev (2011), Schelling (1960, 1966), Goemans (2000), Filson and Werner (2002), Gartzke (2007), and Richardson (1960), as well as against the Kantian tradition of perpetual peace and the balance-of-power tradition from Waltz (1979) through contemporary multipolar concert proposals. The empirical findings of Chojnacki and Reisch (2008) on the typology and escalation dynamics of war provide direct empirical grounding for the formal premises of our model.

title: The P vs NP Constitution: Computational Model Reconstitution in the R³ Paradigm

detail.title: The P vs NP Constitution: Computational Model Reconstitution in the R³ Paradigm
detail.abstract: The P vs NP problem — the central open question in theoretical computer science and one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems — asks whether every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time (NP) can also be solved in polynomial time (P). The question is defined relative to the deterministic Turing machine model of computation. The overwhelming consensus among complexity theorists is that P ≠ NP, but no proof exists in either direction. This paper presents the fifth and final paper of the Russell R³ Constitutional Mathematics series, addressing P vs NP through the fifth and most careful mode of constitutional implementation: computational model reconstitution. The paper makes a precise and bounded claim. It does not assert that P = NP in the standard complexity-theoretic sense — that claim is almost certainly false and is logically unsupported by the argument that bounded blockchain execution compresses exponential search into polynomial time. That argument is explicitly named as an error in Section III of this paper. What the paper claims instead is that complexity classes are model-relative: P and NP are defined with respect to the Turing machine model, and a different computational model — the R³ Bounded Recursive Execution Environment (BREE) — constitutes a different complexity landscape in which the canonical P vs NP distinction does not apply in the same way. The R³ BREE is defined by four properties absent from the Turing machine model: (1) gas-bounded execution — all computations terminate within a fixed resource limit; (2) deterministic replayability — identical inputs always produce identical outputs; (3) immutable ledger recording — every computation is permanently auditable; and (4) ontological grounding — the REFINEMENT_DEPTH bound defines the computational horizon within which problems are decidable. Within the R³ BREE, problems that are NP-hard on a Turing machine may be undecidable (gas-exceeded) rather than exponentially slow — a categorically different relationship between problem structure and resource consumption. This is not P = NP. It is a new complexity theory for a new computational model. The PvsNPDecider_R3 contract is the constitutional document of this new complexity theory. It encodes the R³ BREE complexity commitment, records every decision in a hash-chained Cognitive State Ledger, and inaugurates the open research program that will formalize the R³ BREE complexity hierarchy. The paper names what the contract does, what it does not do, and what the path forward requires.

title: Feasibility Analysis and Business Model Design for the HAMSA Neighborhood Platform: A Social Capital, Sharing Economy, and Neighborhood Governance Approach

detail.title: Feasibility Analysis and Business Model Design for the HAMSA Neighborhood Platform: A Social Capital, Sharing Economy, and Neighborhood Governance Approach
detail.abstract: Economic pressures and the gap between local service supply and demand have intensified interest in community-based digital platforms. This study analyzes the feasibility of "HAMSA," a neighborhood platform integrating skill exchange, resource sharing, group purchasing, peer support, and local education. Using a qualitative, descriptive-analytical method and comparative case studies of global models (Nextdoor, Buy Nothing Project, Time Banking, Community-Supported Agriculture), we find that HAMSA embodies a hybrid logic combining gift economy, time exchange, and local participation. However, practical success depends on field validation, trust mechanisms, and governance. We propose a conceptual model with ten testable hypotheses. This feasibility study concludes that HAMSA is conceptually grounded and socially relevant, but empirical pilot testing is required before implementation.

title: Game Meats Company of Australia v Farm Transparency International Ltd: Two Wrongs Don't Make a (Remedial) Right
affiliations: Monash University - Faculty of Law and

detail.title: Game Meats Company of Australia v Farm Transparency International Ltd: Two Wrongs Don't Make a (Remedial) Right
detail.abstract: Game Meats Company of Australia v Farm Transparency International Ltd raises important questions about the proper limits of discretionary remedialism in Australia. The case arose after the defendant animal rights organisation published footage of the plaintiff's commercial slaughterhouse obtained during several unlawful trespasses. The defendant admitted the trespasses and was ordered to pay the plaintiff general and exemplary damages. The primary judge, however, refused to grant any remedy restraining the defendants from publishing the footage in the future. They also refused to impose a remedial constructive trust over the copyright in the footage, as well as consequent relief requiring transfer of rights in the footage and deletion of it.  On appeal, the Full Federal Court granted the plaintiff a wide range of equitable remedies, including, a remedial constructive trust over the copyright in the footage, largely based on 'unconscionability' and the 'moral calibre' of the defendant's wrongdoing. This article argues that whilst the circumstances in Farm Transparency justified an award of damages in tort, no further remedy was justified or desirable, and the Full Court’s reliance on ‘unconscionability’ or ‘the moral calibre of the wrongdoing’ was misplaced, given the absence of a relevant violated (and unremedied) legal right.

title:
How Much is the Portuguese Language Worth?
An Empirical Valuation Using a High-Dimensional Language-Conditioned Dynamic Asset Valuation Framework (L-DAVF)
affiliations: University of Minho

detail.title:
How Much is the Portuguese Language Worth?
An Empirical Valuation Using a High-Dimensional Language-Conditioned Dynamic Asset Valuation Framework (L-DAVF)
detail.abstract:
We develop and implement the Language-Conditioned Dynamic Asset Valua tion Framework (L-DAVF), the first multi-module econometric system designed to estimate the aggregate economic value of a natural language as an intangible global asset. Applying L-DAVF to Portuguese — the fifth most-spoken language worldwide, spanning the Community of Portuguese Language Countries (CPLP) across four continents — we estimate a time-varying Portuguese Language Value (PLVt) that averages USD 929.9 billion per year over 2000–2023, ranging from USD 293.5 billion (2001) to USD 1,512.2 billion (2011).

The framework integrates five methodological modules: (1) a Dynamic Common Language Exposure Matrix (Lij,t) capturing bilateral language proximity across 46 nodes on 12 components; (2) a Dynamic Language Premium Identification model (DPLPt) using rolling Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) gravity estimation, yielding a mean language trade premium of 6.89% (range: 2.34–11.15%); (3) a Language-Conditioned Multilayer Asset Factor (LAFt) derived from principal component analysis of financial market returns, with a CPLP loading of 0.31; (4) a ShockBridge Pulset measuring language-amplified financial shock transmission, aggregated from 7,558 real rolling-window OLS estimates (mean: 0.367); and (5) a Language Strategic Option Value (LSOVt) priced via a Black-Scholes–CRR ensemble, averaging USD 164.0 billion.

All results are derived exclusively from real, freely accessible market and administrative data. No synthetic or simulated data enters any active code path. The framework is fully documented, reproducible, and open to replication.

title: President Trump's Digital Fort Knox: Reasserting American Financial Leadership through the Commodification of Bitcoin
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: President Trump's Digital Fort Knox: Reasserting American Financial Leadership through the Commodification of Bitcoin

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
President Trump’s Executive Order of 6 March 2025, on the Establishment of the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and
United States Digital Asset Stockpile challenges the traditional role of fiat currency in national security and economic sovereignty. This article examines its geopolitical ramifications, potential to counter central bank digital currencies and implications for US fiscal policy. By positioning Bitcoin as a hedge against inflation and financial weaponisation, President Trump reshapes the debate on monetary autonomy. This article highlights risks, feasibility and the broader shift towards
decentralised financial power.

title: Belief Drift and Directional Inference in English Auctions

detail.title: Belief Drift and Directional Inference in English Auctions
detail.abstract: This paper identifies an interpretation-driven channel of rational learning in commonvalue English auctions. Public dropout actions are mapped into directional signallikelihood events, with truncation events as the benchmark case, and incorporated into a public-history filtration. A single-crossing condition on the net stay advantage provides a primitive source of direction: the canonical case with increasing net stay advantage generates lower-tail exit, whereas environments with sufficiently signalsensitive exit payoffs or participation costs can generate upper-tail exit. Under a monotone likelihood ratio signal structure, lower-tail and upper-tail interpretations generate monotone likelihood tilts of the public posterior. Repeated exits therefore produce systematic downward or upward belief drift. With compact signal support, this drift shifts posterior-based dropout regions, creating new price intervals that support premature exit under downward drift and sustained participation at higher prices under upward drift. A finite-horizon construction illustrates how the reduced-form interpretation weight and dropout schedule can be generated through recursive public-state updating and continuation-value indifference. The mechanism depends on interim public actions and therefore is absent, in the limited filtration-based sense studied here, from Dutch and sealed-bid auctions.

title: From Election Forensics to Lottery Auditing: An Analysis of Korean Lotto 6/45
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: From Election Forensics to Lottery Auditing: An Analysis of Korean Lotto 6/45
detail.abstract: Statistical methods developed for election forensics-including digit-pattern tests, simulation-adjusted chi-square statistics, and summary-statistic variance tests-encode a general logic for detecting non-random structure in sequences of numbers that purport to be drawn uniformly at random. We argue that this logic transfers naturally to the auditing of state-run lotteries, where the fairness guarantee is both mathematically precise and publicly salient. We port, reformulate, and extend eleven tests from the election-forensics literature into a coherent lottery-audit framework, and validate the framework empirically against 1,204 consecutive draws of the Korean Lotto 6/45 (draws 1-1,204). The data are partitioned into five non-overlapping temporal windows to assess epoch-wise stability. The key empirical finding is that while isolated failures occur in five of 75 test-window combinations (6.7%), no single test fails in more than one time window. We show that this non-replication pattern is the appropriate fairness criterion in the presence of inter-test dependence, and that it is far more informative than a naive comparison of observed failures to a multiple-testing expectation computed under a false independence assumption. Beyond the empirical verdict, the paper's primary contribution is the methodological toolkit itself: a reproducible, open-source audit pipeline that any researcher or regulator can apply to any 6/45-style lottery.

title: Cross-Issuer Substitution and Stablecoin Bailouts
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Cross-Issuer Substitution and Stablecoin Bailouts
detail.abstract: Stablecoins issued by different firms are near-perfect substitutes. During runs, users switch between them, supplying private liquidity at no cost to public funds. We show that this substitution channel raises welfare in partial equilibrium but unravels in general equilibrium: each issuer free-rides by correlating its reserves with those of competitors, disabling substitution precisely when it is needed. At calibrated USDC March 2023 parameters, the laissez-faire reserve correlation is 0.75, against a social-planner optimum of 0.01; free-riding erodes three-quarters of the channel's welfare gain. The calibrated system lies near a threshold above which the channel becomes welfare-destroying. Rules that mandate uncorrelated reserves across issuers are therefore necessary, not optional: ex-post bailout commitment alone is inadequate.

title: The Upward-Sloping Path of Fiscal Multipliers and Humped-Persistent Tail Effect: Evidence from a Behavioral New Keynesian Model of South Korea

detail.title: The Upward-Sloping Path of Fiscal Multipliers and Humped-Persistent Tail Effect: Evidence from a Behavioral New Keynesian Model of South Korea
detail.abstract:
This paper estimates a hybrid Behavioral New Keynesian (BNK) model for the South Korean economy, extending the cognitive discounting framework of Gabaix (2020) with a reduced-
form inertia parameter to capture the path dependency characteristic of economies with concentrated illiquid asset holdings. Using Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimation on quarterly Korean macroeconomic data spanning 1991–2025, I identify a cognitive discount factor of approximately 0.74 and a structural inertia weight of 0.44, both significantly different from the US benchmark. The estimated behavioral parameters generate a non-monotonic fiscal multiplier trajectory: an initial dampened response followed by a gradual build-up and a persistent hump — a pattern that departs from the immediate peak and monotonic decay predicted by standard rational expectations models. Robustness checks under alternative expectation assumptions, interest rate regimes, and augmented instrument sets confirm the stability of the estimates. These findings suggest that fiscal policy transmission in Korea operates through a delayed amplification channel rooted in cognitive frictions and structural inertia.

reference: Yesim Atamer and Alexander Hellgardt (eds), Oxford Handbook on Regulatory Contract Law, Oxford University Press, forthcoming
title: Regulating Contracts across Borders: The Role of Private International Law
affiliations: Humboldt University of Berlin

detail.title: Regulating Contracts across Borders: The Role of Private International Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Yesim Atamer and Alexander Hellgardt (eds), Oxford Handbook on Regulatory Contract Law, Oxford University Press, forthcoming

detail.abstract: Private international law – or conflict of laws, as it is commonly referred to in the United States – deals with the co-existence of different legal systems and determines which state’s law applies (should apply) in cross-border cases. It is traditionally regarded as a rather apolitical and value-neutral field of law. In the 20th century, however, private international law has undergone a “regulatory turn”. The chapter explores the nature, origins and implications of this transformation with a particular focus on European private international law. It argues that private international law today not only coordinates legal systems but actively contributes to the pursuit of regulatory goals. Specifically, it shows that private international law advances regulatory goals in two ways: First, in an indirect fashion through the extension of the spatial reach of substantive rules and through the protection of substantive rules from displacement. And, second, in a direct fashion through the integration of regulatory goals into its very own choice-of-law rules. At the same time, the chapter critically examines the role of party autonomy and argues that, while it supports broader policy objectives such as the functioning of the internal market, it should not be understood as a regulatory instrument in a strict sense, but rather as a form of legal infrastructure. Building on these insights, the chapter highlights the increasing importance of private international law for the effectiveness of national and European regulation in cross-border contexts. It concludes that many contemporary challenges – such as the regulation of digital markets, the fight against climate change and the pursuit of sustainability – can only be effectively addressed if the regulatory function of private international law is fully recognised and appropriately developed.

title: Quantitative Large-scale Performance Evaluation of Energy Management Strategies for Hybrid Energy Storage Systems with a Focus on System Sizing
affiliations: Leibniz University Hannover, Leibniz University Hannover and Leibniz University Hannover

detail.title: Quantitative Large-scale Performance Evaluation of Energy Management Strategies for Hybrid Energy Storage Systems with a Focus on System Sizing
detail.abstract:
This study presents a quantitative performance evaluation of energy management strategies (EMS) for hybrid energy storage systems (HESS) with a focus on system sizing. It addresses the lack of systematic and comparable studies across EMS types.
