detail.abstract: The global antibiotic pipeline faces systemic failure rooted in a fundamental methodological error: target identification is treated as a stochastic search problem rather than a deterministic fixed-point derivation. This paper resolves that error. Through recursive ontological decomposition across seven independent layers — molecular biology, resistance evolution, pharmacology, clinical validation, economic structure, formal verification, and regulatory pathway — and exhaustive pairwise cross-analysis of all 21 layer-pair coherence conditions, we prove that the F0F1 ATP synthase subunit C is the unique fixed point of axiomatic coherence in the antibiotic target space. The resulting constitutional framework formally guarantees: broad-spectrum efficacy ≥ 0.94 across 11 clinically critical bacterial species; resistance emergence probability Pescape ≤ 2.5 × 10−15 (Compton-class safety bound); a subscription-based economic model with provably positive net present value; and a pre-specified regulatory pathway qualifying for QIDP designation and Priority Review. This is not a probabilistic estimate. It is a mathematical necessity.

title: When Does ESG Lose Value Relevance? A Discount-Rate Threshold

detail.title: When Does ESG Lose Value Relevance? A Discount-Rate Threshold
detail.abstract: Whether ESG performance creates value for shareholders remains contested. We ask whether the ESG-firm value relation in Korea depends on the prevailing monetary regime. Hansen's (1999) panel threshold model, applied to 5,110 firm-year observations of KOSPI-listed firms over 2012-2025 with cluster-robust inference and 1,000 bootstrap replications, locates a structural break at a 3-year AA-corporate bond yield of 3.19%. The threshold is sharply identified (F = 72.59, bootstrap p < 0.001) and falls between the Bank of Korea's pre-tightening years and the 2022-2024 hiking cycle. The ESG slope is positive below the threshold (β = 0.0147) and negative above it (β =-0.0262), though neither clears the 10% level (p = 0.398; p = 0.151). We read the evidence as a regime shift in how the Korean market prices ESG, in line with the long-duration discount-rate channel in Pástor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2021). The within-regime imprecision matches the rating-noise mechanism in Avramov et al. (2022).

title: Between Truth, Victory, and Timing: Retrospectics as a Strategically Delayed Discursive Intervention

detail.title: Between Truth, Victory, and Timing: Retrospectics as a Strategically Delayed Discursive Intervention
detail.abstract: Organizational decision-making processes are commonly described through two familiar discursive logics: a dialectical orientation toward insight and an eristic orientation toward victory. While this distinction is analytically useful, it remains insufficient for capturing communicative patterns in leadership, strategy, and power contexts whose effectiveness derives less from argumentative superiority than from temporal positioning. This paper conceptually examines and theoretically situates such a pattern: strategically delayed discursive interventions, in which actors initially engage in observation, restraint, or selective visibility before positioning themselves with increased influence during later, socially condensed, or cognitively fatigued phases of discourse. To consolidate this pattern conceptually, the term retrospectics is proposed. Retrospectics does not describe mere restraint, introversion, or classical moderation, but a specific form of discursive influence in which timing, status, observational advantage, and interpretative framing interact. The paper situates this pattern within organizational psychology through the lenses of speaker status, perceptual psychology, social fatigue, decision architecture, and informal authority, while selectively integrating perspectives from sociology and organization theory where these clarify how discursive influence becomes socially legitimized. Retrospectics is explicitly not introduced as a closed theory or validated psychometric construct, but as a cautious conceptual proposal intended to make an observable yet previously diffuse organizational pattern more precisely describable.

title: Inclusionary Regimes, Firm Size, and Housing Approval by Cities
affiliations: University of New Mexico

detail.title: Inclusionary Regimes, Firm Size, and Housing Approval by Cities
detail.abstract: Municipal permitting is a procedural tool that city officials can use to facilitate housing development. City officials control housing permitting in their jurisdiction, but state law ultimately delimits their authority. Using data at the municipal level, the present study examines the likelihood of US municipal governments approving permits for single-family or multifamily units. The study examines panel data on municipal permits for housing and inclusionary regimes. It presents annual data on state preemptions of inclusionary zoning compiled from the Local Solutions Support Center, state statutes, and court rulings identified on a case-by-case basis. Panel data for state preemptions is an original contribution from this research to the literature. The findings suggest that state preemptions of inclusionary zoning have varying impacts on the municipal approval of single-family and multifamily production. The study bridges local government literature and the public/private distinction framework to explain differences in housing units permitted by cities.

title: Narrating Innovation in the Post-plausibility Era: Generative AI, Multimodal Pre-enactment, and the Case of Nikola Corporation

detail.title: Narrating Innovation in the Post-plausibility Era: Generative AI, Multimodal Pre-enactment, and the Case of Nikola Corporation
detail.abstract:
This article explores the shifting nature of communicative creativity in language-
intensive professional practices, specifically within strategic investor communication.
Using the rise and fall of Nikola Corporation as a seminal case study, it first
deconstructs the human creative agency involved in crafting multimodal pre-
enactments—discursive practices that simulate future technological realities to build
trust and market value. The analysis shows how human-led promissory narratives
use linguistic and visual innovation to bridge epistemic gaps, establishing a
benchmark for professional competence in pre-AI strategic communication.
The study then contrasts this human-centric creativity with the rise of Generative AI
(GenAI). It argues that as GenAI reduces the marginal cost of producing highly
plausible multimodal content to near zero, the “creative spark” of entrepreneurial
storytelling undergoes a radical transformation. In this emerging post-plausibility era,
the creative labor of professional communication shifts from the generative ability to
simulate reality toward a higher-order evaluative and ethical competence, positioning
trust as the primary strategic asset in an era of synthetic abundance. By analyzing
the Nikola Paradox, the article illustrates how the automation of strategic persuasion
leads to systemic skepticism, ultimately requiring a reconfiguration of professional
identity and a return to proof of physicality. The study proposes that in a GenAI-
saturated landscape, pre-enactment must be reframed as a transparently creative
vision, distinct from evidentiary claims. Through the introduction of a multidimensional
framework for evaluating promissory narratives, this research contributes to applied
linguistics by conceptualizing professional creativity not as the mere generation of
content, but as the strategic navigation of trust and authenticity in increasingly
mediated financial markets. Structurally, the article unfolds from a foundational
analysis of human narrative construction toward a critical examination of the GenAI
inflection point in Chapter 6, ultimately concluding in a conceptual model for verifying
credibility through physical evidence in Chapter 7.

title: The Devil's Dilemma: Justice or Security in Post-conflict Sudan A Comprehensive Review
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Devil's Dilemma: Justice or Security in Post-conflict Sudan A Comprehensive Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the sole writer and that is my country
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the foundational trade-off between accountability for atrocity crimes and the
urgent need to end armed violence—what Sudanese civil society terms the “Devil’s Dilemma”
(مأزق الشيطان). Focusing on the prospective surrender or negotiation of the Rapid Support Forces
(RSF) in Sudan’s ongoing civil war (2023–2026), the paper develops a theoretical and comparative
framework for analyzing whether, when, and how states may lawfully and legitimately offer
conditional amnesties or reduced sentences to perpetrators of war crimes, crimes against humanity,
and genocide. Drawing on the jurisprudence of the Special Court for Sierra Leone, the evolving
customary international law debate on amnesties, and the transitional justice experiences of South
Africa (Truth and Reconciliation Commission), Rwanda (gacaca courts), Colombia (Special
Jurisdiction for Peace), Liberia (Charles Taylor), Sierra Leone (Lomé Accord), and six original
Sudanese case studies (1999 Amnesty Law; 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement; 2019–2021
transition; 2021 coup; 2020 Juba Peace Agreement; El Geneina massacres), the paper argues that
unconditional amnesty is legally impermissible and politically dangerous, while blanket rejection
of any accommodation is practically catastrophic. The paper proposes a middle-path model of
“conditional acceptance,” comprising targeted ICC surrender of senior leadership, strict vetting,
and DDR with judicial oversight, full truth-telling under oath, reparations financed from
perpetrators’ assets, and GPS-monitored behavioral restrictions. Four analytical tables and three
detailed scenarios (optimistic, pessimistic, and most likely) project the outcomes of different policy
choices. The conclusion argues that the only unforgivable error in Sudan is to pretend that the
choice is easy. That delayed justice is not abandoned justice if the delay saves lives.

title: QUANTIFYING THE SYSTEM VALUE OF DISTRIBUTED SOLAR: A COMPONENT-BASED FRAMEWORK USING UTILITY-SCALE DATA
affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Jordan University of Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering

detail.title: QUANTIFYING THE SYSTEM VALUE OF DISTRIBUTED SOLAR: A COMPONENT-BASED FRAMEWORK USING UTILITY-SCALE DATA
detail.abstract: Distributed photovoltaic (PV) capacity in the United States has expanded rapidly in recent years and is expected to continue growing as solar represents a large share of new electricity-generation additions. Net Energy Metering (NEM) has historically been the dominant policy mechanism used to compensate and incentivize distributed PV adoption. As of 2025, at least 44 U.S. states have enacted some form of net-metering policy, although several jurisdictions have transitioned to successor tariffs or alternative compensation structures [1]. Recent policy activity indicates that nearly all states are actively revisiting distributed solar compensation frameworks, with dozens of regulatory actions addressing revisions to NEM, solar valuation studies, and rate-design reforms [1]. Concerns motivating these investigations include the extent to which retail-rate NEM reflects the system value of distributed PV and whether it creates potential cost-shift equity issues among customers. To support the development of compensation frameworks that more accurately reflect the grid value of distributed PV, this paper develops a transparent, consistent, and repeatable component-based Value of Solar (VoS) methodology. The proposed framework quantifies key value streams associated with distributed PV and is applied using actual operational and planning data from a large investor-owned utility in the Midwestern United States, including distribution system models for two major operating regions within the utility’s service territory. First, we used that utility’s 2025 NEM compensation rules and studied the distributed energy resource billing data and tariff documentation, and established a baseline for NEM, that systems interconnected prior to 2025 receive a 16.09 ¢/kWh bill credit. Second, we calculated the avoided energy component using 8,760-hour locational marginal prices (LMPs) combined with hourly PV generation derived from area-specific irradiance data. Third, we calculated VoS components that include avoided generation capacity, avoided transmission capacity, avoided distribution capacity, and environmental benefits. Results indicate a total VoS of 12.55 ¢/kWh, with energy and environmental benefits representing the largest contributions. A sensitivity analysis shows that the effective load carrying capability (ELCC) and the distribution loss factor are the most influential parameters. The results demonstrate that the proposed methodology provides a defensible and transparent framework for distributed solar valuation that can support regulatory decision-making and future compensation mechanism design.

title: Anchored Intrinsic Coordinates for Grokking: Curvature, Predictive Reducibility, and Boundary Cases
affiliations: Clevix AI Research

detail.title: Anchored Intrinsic Coordinates for Grokking: Curvature, Predictive Reducibility, and Boundary Cases
detail.abstract: We study the geometry of grokking trajectories in normalised intrinsic coordinates (u, w), where u rescales log V t between memorisation and validation-transition reference points and w rescales the angular displacement α t from the memorisation direction. Reading the postmemorisation dynamics through the lens of fast-slow systems, we ask whether grokking trajectories collapse onto a 1-D slow manifold in (u, w), with structured deviations diagnostic of where the reduction breaks down. Five complementary findings emerge from 204 trajectories spanning 5 architectures, 2 modular arithmetic tasks, 6 hyperparameter cells per architecture, 3 seeds per cell, and 24 sparse-parity trajectories as a negative control. (F1) First-order affine backbone on three architectures. On 1L Transformer, 3L Transformer, and MLP shallow, the empirical shape follows the constant-rate slowmanifold limit w ≈ 1-u: per-architecture per-trajectory mean slope lies in [-1.05,-0.97] and intercept in [+0.94, +0.99], with per-trajectory R 2 mean ≥ 0.88. Three independent null models (random-monotone, within-trajectory u-w decoupling, and cross-trajectory profile swap) consistently support identifiability: 90.8% of empirical trajectories below the random-monotone null median, 100% below the decoupling null median, and 49.2% on the cross-trajectory swap test (≈ 50%, the outcome supporting intra-family shape consistency). (F2) Second-order curvature correction across all five architectures. The residual u + w-1 exhibits a systematic concave-down deviation pattern (CDP): the median residual is negative for u ∈ [0.3, 0.7] on every architecture (range-0.18 to-0.06), opposite to the random-monotone null (+0.17), and qualitatively consistent with a perturbative correction (Corollary 2) under bell-shaped empirical G(α). The important finding is not exact linearity but the structured failure of linearity: F2 is more architecture-robust than F1 in the sense that the architecture that least supports F1 (MLP deep) exhibits the largest CDP magnitude. (F3, negative control) Path-length separation. The integrated path length L combined separates grokked modular trajectories from sparse-parity trajectories with zero overlap (separation factor 9.22×, Mann-Whitney p = 3.91 • 10-11); sparse parity has no contraction phase and correctly fails to produce a shape function. (F4) Predictive content. Fitting Corollary 2's first-order G(α) on the first 20% of post-memorisation trajectory and forward-integrating predicts log V ⋆ within 5-31% relative error on 4 of 6 architectures (best: MLP shallow, 4.9%, 8.3× tighter than naive). (F5) Manifold single-valuedness diagnostic. We define SVI = 1-E[Var(w | u)]/Var(w) as a coordinate-aware test of slow-manifold reducibility. Computed at three scales (per-trajectory, within-cell, pooled), SVI cleanly separates 5 architectures with robust slow-manifold reducibility (SVI ≥ 0.90 at every scale) from MLP deep (0.975 per-trajectory but 0.573 pooled), revealing MLP deep's boundary behaviour as cell-dependence of the manifold's parametrisation rather than its absence. F5 unifies four previously disconnected MLP-deep observations (slope-1.16, largest CDP, lowest R 2 , smallest F4 advantage) as projections of one underlying property. A 12-cell sensitivity grid over post-hoc thresholds confirms F1 robustness; we pre-register a 7-criterion audit and all seven pass.

detail.abstract:
The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline represents a major shift in national behavioral health crisis policy by creating a universally accessible three-digit number for individuals experiencing mental health emergencies. However, while 988 established a nationally recognized access point, the infrastructure supporting crisis response remains uneven across states and regions. This working paper argues that the primary limitation of the 988 system is not conceptual, but operational. Specifically, fragmented implementation structures, inconsistent backend crisis infrastructure, workforce shortages, technological limitations, and geographic disparities continue to shape the quality and continuity of crisis response across the United States.

Drawing upon implementation theory, comparative state analysis, and emerging crisis response data, this paper examines how disparities in funding mechanisms, mobile crisis availability, stabilization infrastructure, and operational readiness create unequal access to behavioral health crisis services. The paper further explores how geographic fragmentation and increasing societal mobility challenge traditional crisis routing frameworks that remain heavily dependent upon localized infrastructure and area-code-based systems.

In addition, this paper introduces maternal mental health and postpartum depression as a high-need population lens through which broader implementation inequities become particularly visible. By examining the intersection of crisis governance, infrastructure equity, and vulnerable populations, this research argues that 988 should be understood not merely as a hotline policy but as a national crisis infrastructure policy.

Ultimately, this paper contends that the long-term success of 988 will depend on whether policymakers are willing to move beyond symbolic policy adoption and invest in coordinated, equitable, and modernized crisis response systems capable of delivering meaningful intervention regardless of geography.

title:
Stable Matchings
An Analysis of the Stable Marriage, Hospitals/Residents and Stable Roommates Problems

detail.title:
Stable Matchings
An Analysis of the Stable Marriage, Hospitals/Residents and Stable Roommates Problems
detail.abstract:
This project aims to introduce the Stable Marriage Problem, the Hospitals/Residents Prob-
lem and the Stable Roommates Problem along with their most relevant properties and appli-
cations.
     The Stable Marriage Problem considers two equally sized sets of men and women, where
each man is looking to marry a woman and each woman is looking to marry a man. Each
person has a strictly ordered list of their preferences and the goal is to obtain a stable marriage
or as it will be called, a stable matching. A stable matching is a one-to-one pairing between
the set of men and the set of women with no man and woman who would leave their assigned
pair to marry each other. We introduce an algorithm that finds stable matchings and we show
that there can be a multitude of stable matchings. We explore their properties and consider
what matchings would be advantageous to the men or the women, how many stable matchings
can there be and how can different stable matchings be related to each other. We prove these
results and illustrate them through explicit examples.
     The Hospitals/Residents Problem can be described as an extension of the Stable Marriage
Problem. It considers a set of medical school students that have to be matched to a set of
hospitals for their residency. While each resident is matched to exactly one hospital, each
hospital will be matched with at least one student. The criterion for stability is equivalent
to the case of the Stable Marriage Problem. We introduce two algorithms that find stable
matchings for this problem. We prove comparable results for the Hospitals/Residents Problem
akin to those of the Stable Marriage Problem and illustrate them through thorough examples.
      The Stable Roommates Problem is a generalisation of the Stable Marriage Problem. It
considers a single set containing an even number of people, where each person ranks everyone
else in a preference list and needs to be matched with someone else in the same set. A matching
entails dividing the set into separate pairs with no overlap and it is considered unstable when
there exist two persons that are not matched to each other, each of whom prefers the other over
their respective partners in the matching. We use the properties described in the section on
the Stable Marriage Problem to construct a two-phase algorithm that finds stable matchings
for this problem. We prove the most fundamental properties and apply the framework of the
Stable Roommates Problem in a scenario that involves matching coworkers on projects based
on their work performance. The scenario aims to enquire ways for a company to match their
employees in a way that maximises productivity.

title: Owning With Style: How Corporate Owners Shape Firm Strategy
affiliations: Wharton School, University of Penn

detail.title: Owning With Style: How Corporate Owners Shape Firm Strategy

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support from the Mack Institute for Innovation Management is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: While management research traditionally views corporate owners as governance actors, recent work suggests they also drive complex organizational change that requires distinct capabilities to implement. I investigate how owners implement their strategy across portfolio firms by examining employee mobility within private equity portfolios. Using career history and work activity data for over 8.7 million employees across 12,775 firms receiving first-ever private equity investment in 2001-2021, I document three findings. First, following investment, portfolio firms increase hiring from their new owner's prior portfolio firms, particularly into managerial, finance, and operations roles. Second, this common-owner hiring is more prevalent under owners who emphasize strategic growth, and less prevalent under those focused on financial engineering. Third, a firm's organizational focus converges toward that of other firms in the same portfolio after investment, but primarily when the firm also hires common-owner employees. These findings indicate a relational mechanism through which owners shape firms: they build a network of trusted talent and deploy it into new portfolio firms to implement their owner-specific strategy.

title: Linking Innovation Barriers to Innovation Activities: Evidence from South Korea’s Manufacturing Sector

detail.title: Linking Innovation Barriers to Innovation Activities: Evidence from South Korea’s Manufacturing Sector

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/IER/30/01/01
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 31 No. 1, pp. 6-16

detail.abstract:
This study assesses the evolving innovation climate of South Korea’s manufacturing industry by examining the relationship between perceived innovation barriers and innovation activities. Using firm-level microdata from the Korean Innovation Survey covering the period from 2020 to 2024, the analysis reveals a post-pandemic paradox: a heightened perception of innovation barriers has coexisted with a significant increase in overall innovation activity.

However, this aggregate trend masks a critical divergence based on technological intensity. For firms in the low-technology sector, the results support a “revealed barrier” effect, in which heightened barrier perception stems from persistent engagement in innovation.

Conversely, for firms in the high-technology sector, barriers act as genuine “Deterrents,” with financial and market constraints significantly reducing innovation success rates. These findings suggest that a one-size-fits-all policy approach is insufficient. The study concludes that innovation policy must be bifurcated: focusing on de-risking financial and market uncertainties for high-technology sectors, while addressing operational and capability frictions for low-technology sectors.

title: First-Passage Prediction of Grokking Delay: A Calibrated Law under AdamW with Causal Validation
affiliations: Clevix AI Research, , Clevix AI Research and State Bank of Vietnam - Banking Academy of Vietnam

detail.title: First-Passage Prediction of Grokking Delay: A Calibrated Law under AdamW with Causal Validation
detail.abstract:
We give the first quantitative prediction of grokking delay under AdamW: a closed-form first-passage law with MAPE 17.7% on 26 held-out runs spanning a 41× delay range, with mechanism causally validated. The result fits a unified picture of delayed generalisation as a crossing problem in the joint (V t , α t) space of parameter norm and angular displacement: V t = ∥θ t ∥ 2 contracts exponentially toward an architecture-dependent threshold V ⋆ , while α t must reach an angular threshold α ⋆ , and grokking occurs only when both are reached. The closed-form law, 

                                                       T grok-T mem ≈ 1 2 κ LL ηλ log V mem V ⋆ , 

is calibrated on a single cell by an architecture-level constant κ LL that absorbs the AdamW correction to the clean-SGD rate 2ηλ; MAPE rises to 18.0% across architectures and 23.3% across full cross-task scope (46 runs, 43.5× range), with structured residual identifying V ⋆ /V mem as the comparatively stable invariant within architecture (CV ≈ 14% on 1L). Mechanistic foundation. The joint-crossing picture is supported by (i) a quantile-margin theorem: positive delay requires both norm separation V mem > V post and angular reachability of α ⋆ = arcsin(C/V 1/2 Tmem) with C := M q∆ /G eff ; calibrating C on p = 89 predicts α ⋆ = 47.2 • for p = 97 (observed 47.8 • , error 1.3%); (ii) Block F causal interventions (0/6 grok vs. 3/3 baseline when V t is frozen or λ is removed at T mem), which trap α near 12 • ≪ α ⋆. Concurrent theoretical work (Boursier et al., 2025, Muşat et al., 2025) characterises the post-memorisation dynamics; our contribution is the corresponding prediction theory for AdamW with explicit observables, calibration, and causal tests.

title: Monetary Architecture and the Political Limits of Money Creation
affiliations: and

detail.title: Monetary Architecture and the Political Limits of Money Creation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no known financial interests, personal relationships, or competing interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The analysis is based exclusively on publicly available aggregate government finance statistics and does not involve human participants, personal data, or identifiable individual information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary debates on sovereign money creation remain divided between orthodox frameworks emphasizing debt sustainability and inflationary constraints and Modern Monetary Theory (MMT), which emphasizes the operational monetary sovereignty of currency-issuing states subject primarily to real resource constraints. This paper argues that both traditions insufficiently theorize the institutional and fiscal structures through which sovereign expenditure is absorbed within the political economy.

To address this gap, the paper introduces the concept of Monetary Architecture (MA), defined as the institutional, fiscal, political, and regulatory structures through which sovereign fiscal activity is allocated, transmitted, absorbed, and legitimized. The framework argues that similar levels of sovereign spending may generate sharply different outcomes depending on how fiscal absorption is organized. In some systems, sovereign expenditure becomes capacity-expanding by reinforcing human development, productive integration, domestic multipliers, and absorptive capacity. In others, it becomes structurally dissipative through fragmentation, external leakage, debt-service burdens, and weak productive transmission mechanisms.

The framework is operationalized through the Social Contract Ratio (SCR) and its adjusted variant (aSCR), which measure the developmental orientation of fiscal absorption using standardized COFOG expenditure classifications. Comparative illustrations ranging from Nordic welfare states to debt-compressed economies demonstrate how divergent fiscal architectures condition developmental absorption across heterogeneous political economies. The analysis further suggests that inflationary fragility and monetary stability emerge partly from the institutional capacity of fiscal systems to transform sovereign expenditure into productive and absorptive expansion.

By shifting analytical attention from the quantity of sovereign spending toward the institutional architecture governing its absorption, the framework contributes to debates in MMT, development economics, fiscal sociology, and comparative political economy across both advanced economies and the Global South.

title: Index Policies for Advance Scheduling
affiliations: University of Miami - Department of Management Science, University of Miami - Department of Management Science and University of Miami - Department of Management Science

detail.title: Index Policies for Advance Scheduling
detail.abstract: We study a finite-horizon advance scheduling problem in which stochastic arrivals must be assigned online to service dates within a rolling booking window. The objective is to minimize the expected total cost generated by current service load and deferred workload across the window. The problem leads to a high-dimensional dynamic program because each booking decision couples all future positions through a per-period demand balance constraint. We address this difficulty through a Lagrangian relaxation approach that reveals a recursively linked family of one-dimensional subproblems and yields a simple closed-loop index policy. In a large-demand regime where arrivals and costs scale linearly with system size while the horizon and booking window length remain fixed, we prove an (O(1)) total gap to a Lagrangian lower bound, which translates into an (O(1/n)) per-unit optimality gap. Numerical experiments show that the policy performs well even at moderate scales. The same Lagrangian relaxation framework extends to service caps with rejection and to cancellations, where experiments provide numerical support for the corresponding conjectured large-scale behavior.

title:
Trips, Territory, and the Digital Trade Deficit:
Rethinking Intellectual Property Rights and e-commerce

detail.title:
Trips, Territory, and the Digital Trade Deficit:
Rethinking Intellectual Property Rights and e-commerce
detail.abstract:
The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights was concluded in 1994. That sentence, unremarkable on its face, carries considerable jurisprudential weight: the negotiators at Marrakesh had no occasion to consider software-as-a-service, no framework for algorithmic content generation, and no appreciation of what a globally interconnected server architecture would do to territorially organised enforcement. The WTO Work Programme on Electronic Commerce, initiated in 1998, recognised many of these emerging difficulties, the uncertain classification of electronically transmitted products, the growing impossibility of confining infringement to a single jurisdiction, the absence from TRIPS of any provision
specifically addressing intermediary liability. A quarter-century of subsequent deliberation has not
resolved them.

This paper argues that the central difficulty is structural rather than incidental. TRIPS was designed around a territorial premise, that rights are granted by states, enforced by courts with territorial jurisdiction, and violated by identifiable acts in identifiable places. Digital commerce dissolves each of those assumptions simultaneously. The paper examines this structural misfit across copyright, patent, trademark, geographical indications, enforcement, and data governance, and assesses what the July 2024 Joint Statement Initiative on Electronic Commerce does, and conspicuously does not, contribute to resolving it.

reference: INSEAD Working Paper No. 2026/28/EFE
title: LBO Debt Package Structuring: From Classic Syndicated Structures to the Age of Private Credit
affiliations: INSEAD - Singapore, INSEAD, INSEAD and INSEAD

detail.title: LBO Debt Package Structuring: From Classic Syndicated Structures to the Age of Private Credit
detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural evolution of leveraged buyout (LBO) debt structuring from the classic multitranche bank-syndicated model of the pre-2008 era through the private credit-dominated landscape of 2026. While existing work has tended to address individual components of LBO financing in relative isolation, this paper integrates instrument architecture, covenant design, and interest rate sensitivity within a unified analytical framework spanning three distinct market eras. Drawing on industry market data, regulatory filings, and practitioner-oriented analysis [adjust to reflect your actual sources], the paper traces how three structural forces-post-GFC regulatory reform (Basel III and the Volcker Rule), a decade of zero interest rate policy (ZIRP), and the emergence of scaled private credit platforms-fundamentally reshaped the traditional architecture of term loan A/B tranches, high yield bonds, and mezzanine debt, and enabled the rise of direct lending and the unitranche as the defining instruments of modern LBO finance. The paper documents covenant evolution across three distinct eras: from full quarterly maintenance packages, to cov-lite incurrence-only structures in the broadly syndicated loan (BSL) market, to the single net leverage test that characterises most private credit facilities today. Central to the analysis is the explicit modelling of interest rate sensitivity across three rate environments-the ZIRP decade (2010-2021), the peak rate shock (2022-2023), and the new normal (2024-2026)-illustrating how SOFR levels directly constrain leverage multiples and equity returns. The paper also analyses the geographic expansion of private credit into European mid-markets and its move into large-cap transactions via club deal structures. A structured decision framework for the 2026 deal team is presented, together with an identification of six common structuring pitfalls. The paper concludes that while instruments, market structure, and rate environments have undergone profound transformation, three enduring principles remain unchanged: seniority determines cost, coverage ratios constrain debt capacity, and leverage amplifies both gains and losses.

title: Avoid the Middle: Public Market Costs, Governance Exemptions, and Capital Formation
affiliations: and Colorado State University, Fort Collins - Department of Finance & Real Estate

detail.title: Avoid the Middle: Public Market Costs, Governance Exemptions, and Capital Formation
detail.abstract: Why do small public firms manage their public float around regulatory thresholds? We exploit the 2018 SEC amendment that raised the Smaller Reporting Company (SRC) threshold from $75 million to $250 million while leaving the SOX Section 404(b) exemption threshold unchanged at $75 million. This allows us to distinguish whether threshold avoidance is driven by governance or disclosure incentives. Firms already below $75 million, retaining both benefits, continue to bunch at the threshold and show significant post-reform increases in equity issuance, capital expenditures, and patenting. Firms newly eligible only for scaled disclosure show no such response. Our results suggest that the SOX Section 404(b) governance exemption, not scaled disclosure, is the primary driver of public float management among small public firms, and have important implications for the design of size-based securities regulation.

detail.abstract: This article provides a sociological analysis of the representations held by individuals in Algerian society regarding age and the body. It highlights the importance of studying this issue within the social tensions between two perspectives characterizing "Global South" societies: traditional culture and globalized culture. The value system governing Algerian society is considered the primary factor in these tensions ; however, digital media has emerged as a powerful variable influencing the construction of social outlooks, reflected in the behaviors of individuals within the social sphere. This article draws on the academic theoretical framework concerning these representations and the variables governing their construction within the processes of social transformation in Algerian society specifically, and within the structure of African societies that represent an identity-historical extension of Algerian society.

title: Research Participation as a Predictor of Postgraduate Study Intentions among Undergraduates in Nigerian Public Universities
affiliations: University of Uyo, University of Calabar Calabar and University of Uyo (UNIUYO)

detail.title: Research Participation as a Predictor of Postgraduate Study Intentions among Undergraduates in Nigerian Public Universities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest is declared by the authors
declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained from all individuals included in this study
declarations.funderStatement: There is no funding to this research work

detail.abstract: This study examined the extent to which research participation and academic motivation jointly predict postgraduate study intentions among undergraduates in public universities in Nigeria. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behaviour and Human Capital Theory, the study posited that both predictors would significantly influence students' aspirations for advanced education. A predictive correlational research design was adopted. The target population comprised 53,027 regular undergraduate students (years three to final year) across public universities in Nigeria. Using a priori power analysis (95% statistical power; d = 0.50), a sample of 382 participants was selected through proportionate stratified random sampling. Two researcher-developed instruments the Research Participation and Academic Motivation Questionnaire (RPAMQ) and the Postgraduate Study Intentions Questionnaire (PGSIQ) were administered. Instruments demonstrated acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .82-.86). Multiple regression analysis was employed to test the stated hypothesis. Undergraduate students exhibited low levels of research participation (M = 1.90), academic motivation (M = 1.94), and postgraduate study intentions (M = 1.82), all falling below the criterion mean of 2.50. The joint regression model was statistically significant (R² = .603; F(2, 379) = 287.91, p < .001), with research participation and academic motivation collectively explaining approximately 60.3% of the variance in postgraduate study intentions. However, disaggregated analysis revealed that academic motivation was the sole statistically significant individual predictor (β = .777, p < .001), while research participation did not independently contribute to postgraduate study intentions (β = .013, p = .699). The study was limited to selected public universities in Nigeria, which may constrain the generalizability of findings. Future research should investigate the moderating roles of gender, discipline, and socioeconomic status, and employ longitudinal designs to track the development of postgraduate intentions across academic years.

title: Hurricane Beryl and the Problem of Restoring Essential Functions: A Preparedness-Centered Disaster Response Architecture Author

detail.title: Hurricane Beryl and the Problem of Restoring Essential Functions: A Preparedness-Centered Disaster Response Architecture Author

detail.abstract: Disasters differ in origin, but many converge operationally when affected populations remain without such essential functions as safe water, power for priority loads, usable shelter, communications, and medical continuity. Among the disaster-response variables most susceptible to preparedness-centered improvement, latency in restoring these functions is plausibly one of the highest-leverage targets. Additional resources matter, but only insofar as they can be converted into executable capability at the point of need. This paper uses Hurricane Beryl as a worked case of essential-function restoration latency. Beryl exposed severe disruption across access, logistics, communications, energy, shelter, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), public health, transport, and stabilization in island and remote-community settings. Public response and follow-up materials point not merely to a need for more resources, but to faster conversion of information into action, storage into dispatch, transport into access, supplies into usable capability, field reports into retargeted logistics, and response into recovery. The paper proposes Time to First Effective Capability as a primary measure of disaster-response responsiveness: the interval between impact or actionable detection and activation of a needed stabilizing function at the point of need. It then maps Beryl-related operational lessons to module-level innovations in a preparedness-centered disaster-response architecture specified in a companion OSF resource. The analysis remains pre-validation and does not estimate lives saved, morbidity avoided, or recovery acceleration. The empirical question is how much the architecture can reduce restoration latency under degraded and boundary-state conditions.

detail.title: Climate and Prehistoric Migration

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School BGIE Unit Working Paper No. 26-082
publicationDetails.journalName: Harvard Business School: Business, Government & the International Economy Unit Working Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 26-082

detail.abstract: What factors drove human migration before modern states, markets, and borders? We develop a framework of ecological sorting in which climate-specific subsistence knowledge depreciates with ecological distance. To test this, we use ancient DNA identity by descent segments to construct bilateral migration flows across Western Eurasia over the last 10,000 years. We document four main findings. First, migration flows decline with differences in growing degree days, precipitation, and soil characteristics between origins and destinations. Second, the dimensions of climate that bind vary across subsistence systems: farmers exhibit strong thermal and soil matching, while pastoralists match most strongly on precipitation—consistent with differential ecological constraints and limiting factors. Third, periods of warming increase farmer expansion while cooling increases pastoral expansion in patterns that recover known archaeological migration episodes. Migration also acts as a margin of climate adaptation: populations exposed to temperature change move to destinations that partly offset the shift. Fourth, genetic flow predicts subsequent convergence in destination vegetation toward migrants’ ecological profiles, consistent with migration shaping landscape change and the demic diffusion of subsistence practices.

reference: Intertax, volume 50, issue Issue 5, 2022[10.54648/taxi2022028]
title: Uganda's Tax System: Key Challenges and Prospects for Improvement
affiliations: University Leipzig, University Leipzig and

detail.title: Uganda's Tax System: Key Challenges and Prospects for Improvement
detail.abstract: Most studies on tax research have focused on the developed countries, and those on developing countries concentrate on subjects of general application. As a result, research on many aspects of tax applicable to low-income countries (LICs) has been neglected. By presenting an in-depth analysis of Uganda's tax system, this study seeks to address this gap. The authors analysed panel data spanning over seventeen years to identify the key system gaps. The findings revealed that Uganda's tax system conforms to the generally accepted international standards, and its economic performance during the period was above the regional sub-Sahara Africa (SSA) average. However, tax revenue performance still remains poor. The main reasons include: unrealistic tax expenditures, corruption, poor governance, low tax morale, overdependence on international trade tax revenues, and structural system weaknesses. To address those challenges, mitigation measures including creating a firm and all-inclusive political settlement; enforcing anti-corruption measures; streamlining the tax system to eliminate system inefficiencies; and systematically formalizing the agricultural and informal sectors to widen the tax base are proposed. It is hoped that the findings provide valuable insights to tax policymakers in formulating policies for improving revenue performance in Uganda and related LICs.

title: Unilateral Parallel Algorithmic Behaviour in EU Financial Services Law

detail.title: Unilateral Parallel Algorithmic Behaviour in EU Financial Services Law

contentFormat.other: Pre publication paper which will be published on ERA Forum Springer Publications

detail.abstract: Unilateral parallel algorithmic behaviour describes market outcomes in which competing firms, each deploying its own pricing system, converge on supra-competitive prices without agreement, communication, or data sharing. The result is economically indistinguishable from cartel conduct, yet it falls outside Article 101 TFEU as now understood. This article argues that the gap is doctrinal, not merely evidential. It maps the relevant CJEU and national case law, explains why MiFID II, the Market Abuse Regulation, the AI Act, and the DMA do not close the problem, and examines the comparative position in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada. It then proposes a limited reform package aimed at supervision, information, and remedies in EU financial services.

title: The Dissective Diagnosis Protocol: Absence Signals for Cross-Domain Risk Assessment Under Information Asymmetry
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Dissective Diagnosis Protocol: Absence Signals for Cross-Domain Risk Assessment Under Information Asymmetry
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Dissective Diagnosis Protocol (DDP), a practical five-step framework for risk assessment under severe information asymmetry. Developed inductively from over a decade of cross-domain diagnostic experience—in intimate relationships, investment due diligence, organizational turnaround, and cross-border infrastructure—the DDP centers on absence signals: elements that should be present but are missing, which often prove more diagnostic than surface-level information.
The protocol proceeds through five operational steps: (1) Absence Signal Detection; (2) Structural Dissection across strategic, structural, procedural, financial, and behavioral layers; (3) Cross-Domain Experiential Calibration when domain expertise is limited; (4) Break Point Identification; and (5) Actionable Pathway Output with sequenced recommendations and explicit gating conditions.
Two preliminary studies are presented. An 8-week behavioral log study (N=35) in early-stage romantic relationships showed that low Consistency Index strongly predicted breakup (OR = 0.005, p = 0.013), with high conflict and declining trends providing additional warning signals. Six retrospective case studies from business negotiations, organizational diagnosis, and cross-border due diligence further illustrate the framework’s application.
The DDP does not eliminate uncertainty and may generate both false positives and false negatives. It is offered as a provisional tool to support decision-making when domain expertise, validated algorithms, or strong research evidence are unavailable.
Keywords: absence signals, signal detection, risk assessment, decision making under uncertainty, due diligence, cross-domain calibration, organizational diagnosis, behavioral consistency

title: The latent paradox: setpoint demand response in tropical commercial buildings shifts peak load instead of shedding it
affiliations: Ramkhamhaeng University

detail.title: The latent paradox: setpoint demand response in tropical commercial buildings shifts peak load instead of shedding it
detail.abstract: Demand response (DR) in commercial buildings is a low-cost grid-flexibility resource validated extensively in temperate climates, yet its transferability to tropical climates remains unverified. This paper evaluates 13 DR scenarios for a Bangkok medium office over a full-year EnergyPlus simulation under the Metropolitan Electricity Authority Tariff 3.2 time-of-use structure. The scenarios span four canonical DR strategy families: temperature-only setback, pre-cooling, humidity-aware control, and supply-air-temperature reset. Results identify three counter-intuitive findings absent from temperate-climate DR literature. First, temperature setback decreases sensible cooling load by 11.2% under +2 °C all-day setback but simultaneously increases coil latent load by 18.2% via variable-air-volume mass-flow modulation that elevates the outdoor-air fraction in supply air, capping total cooling reduction at 0.3%. Second, peak-only DR strategies shift the annual peak from baseline April afternoon to February cool-morning hours, increasing demand by 1.4–14.9% despite reducing within-event peak. Third, pre-cooling is catastrophic in tropical conditions, increasing annual peak by 46.4% and TOU bill by 2.0%, contrary to its established temperate-climate effectiveness. Humidity-aware control overlays produce no measurable benefit because conventional VAV systems inherently over-dehumidify in tropical SAT regimes. The simplest strategy—uniform +2 °C all-day setback—delivers the largest economic benefit at 7.95% TOU bill savings. Tropical DR programmes should prioritise system-level interventions verified against monthly peak demand rather than event-based strategies imported from temperate-climate templates

title: Normative Influence in Organisational Cybersecurity: The Roles of Authority, MessageValence, and Individual Differences
affiliations: Nottingham Trent University, Nottingham Trent University and Nottingham Trent University

detail.title: Normative Influence in Organisational Cybersecurity: The Roles of Authority, MessageValence, and Individual Differences
detail.abstract: Human factors remain a critical vulnerability in organisational cybersecurity, yetresearch has largely emphasised individual-level determinants. This study examineshow social-contextual mechanisms, including normative influence and messagevalence, shape employees’ engagement with cybersecurity behaviours. Using anexperimental vignette methodology, 301 UK employees evaluated scenarios involvingcommon cybersecurity practices, rating their likelihood of help-seeking, perceivedimportance, future motivation, and perceived risk of non-compliance.Counterproductive work behaviour (CWB), organisational citizenship behaviour (OCB),and qualitative work life inventory (QWLI) were included as covariates.Multilevel analyses showed subjective norms consistently produced the strongesteffects across outcomes, outperforming descriptive and injunctive norms. Positivemessage valence significantly increased help-seeking, perceived importance, and riskperception, whereas authority cues showed weak and inconsistent effects. Individualdifferences were also influential: higher OCB predicted greater engagement, whilehigher CWB predicted reduced engagement and weakened OCB’s positive effects.QWLI showed a selective relationship, with poorer perceived work life associated onlywith higher perceived importance. Interaction effects indicated that positive valenceamplified descriptive and injunctive norms, while subjective norms remained robustregardless of framing.These findings highlight the primacy of social influence and message framing overhierarchical authority in shaping cybersecurity intentions, suggesting organisationsshould prioritise peer norms, positive communication, and supportive climates overtop-down or fear-based approaches.

title: Public Trust and Transparency Building Public Trust in Governance: Lessons for Armenia from Finland

detail.title: Public Trust and Transparency Building Public Trust in Governance: Lessons for Armenia from Finland
detail.abstract: This thesis investigates the transferability of Finnish governance best practices to address transparency, accountability, and public trust deficits within the Armenian public administration. Utilizing a qualitative research design with purposive sampling, data was gathered through semi structured interviews with six key institutional and civil society stakeholders from both Finland and Armenia. Thematic analysis reveals that while Armenia has established foundational legal frameworks for open governance, its existing mechanisms remain fragmented, reactive, and heavily dependent on localized leadership. In contrast, Finland’s exceptionally high levels of institutional trust stem from deep rooted, systemic routines such as proactive transparency, strict rule of law enforcement, merit based open recruitment, and structured civic engagement. The study concludes that cultural variations are not primary barriers to governance reform. Rather, the strategic adoption of core procedural routines, including the establishment of a centralized digital transparency platform to consolidate public data, can successfully reduce administrative uncertainty and structurally rebuild sustainable public trust in Armenia.
